📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Industry Voices—The case for social prescribing in older adult care" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Loneliness and social isolation often show up in the exam room through an older patient’s high blood pressure, worsening depression or recent emergency department visit.

Lack of social connection is an increasingly common risk factor for both physical and mental health conditions that clinicians often recognize—but may not feel well-equipped to treat.

Approximately one in four older Americans is socially isolated, and more than four in 10 report feeling lonely. Both are associated with high rates of morbidity and mortality, including elevated risks of heart disease, stroke, cognitive decline and dementia. Social isolation is also associated with an additional $6.7 billion in Medicare spending, mainly from avoidable hospital and nursing home utilization.

It has been revealed that as leaders of foundations committed to improving the health and well-being of older adults, we invest heavily in programs that foster social connection, especially for underserved populations. But to truly address this public health epidemic, healthcare providers must be part of the solution.

Clinicians can play an essential role in identifying lonely and isolated patients and referring them to resources that promote social engagement. Integrating social prescribing into clinical workflows presents challenges in the current U.S. payment system, but promising approaches are showing success and can be replicated.

Food as Medicine (FAM) programs have already expanded our understanding of what a prescription can encompass. While physicians regularly recommend that patients adopt a healthy diet, that advice is rarely heeded for both behavioral and socioeconomic reasons. What has made a difference is a clinician’s prescribing of free or affordable individualized interventions in partnership with community-based resources and with systemwide support.

Similarly, social prescribing is a structured, team-based intervention that involves assessing and addressing loneliness and social isolation as part of a patient’s care blueprint. Taking the patient’s individualized needs and circumstances into account, a referral is made to a community organization or program that fosters social connections. These activities can range from in-person group programs to virtual activities or telephone-based companionship for people with mobility or transportation barriers.

In the United Kingdom (U.K.), Canada and Australia, established social prescribing programs have been linked to reductions in emergency department visits, hospitalizations and healthcare spending.

It has been revealed that brief, validated assessment tools, such as the UCLA-3-Item Loneliness Scale and the condensed Berkman-Syme Social Network Index, can be incorporated into the routine patient health questionnaires to help identify those at risk. Hospitals have a fresh incentive to use these screens with the recently implemented Age-Friendly Hospital Measure from the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services, which includes addressing social vulnerability as one of five required domains.

In a recent development, but what then? Identifying suitable programs, partnering with local organizations, and making those connections for patients is a job in itself, one that clinicians cannot reasonably be expected to add to their already full workload. And this is especially complicated in rural areas where both clinicians and programs are more likely to be limited.

It has been revealed that in the U.K., they have designated “link workers” to fill this role. Here in the U.S., value-based care team practices, which are becoming more common, can support a similar position or share those responsibilities among team members. A Social Prescribing Learning Hub from Social Prescribing USA offers practical guidance for how providers can get started, including choosing community partners and models, measuring impact and navigating the insurance landscape.

Industry observers note that the state of Connecticut has taken a different approach by building a social prescribing infrastructure in collaboration with SocialRx, a tech giant that matches patients with appropriate programs, enabling healthcare providers to prescribe participation in arts and cultural activities that are free to state residents. Other states, including Georgia, Massachusetts and California, have developed similar social prescribing ecosystems.

It has been revealed that some insurers and care providers are creating their own social connection programs. BCBS of Massachusetts has partnered with Elder Services of Worcester Area to reduce emergency department utilization among their Medicare Advantage members by providing Transition Coaches after hospitalizations or ED visits. The coaches screen patients for isolation and loneliness, connect them with social groups and companion visits, and help them use technology to stay connected with family, friends and healthcare providers.

Building a sustainable social prescribing infrastructure also requires government and philanthropic support for evidence-based programs that foster social connections in spaces where older adults commonly gather. One example is the American Library Association’s Aging Together initiative, supported by The John A. Hartford Foundation, which strengthens public library programs that reduce social isolation and promote older adults' health and well-being.

It has been revealed that other countries’ experience with social prescribing is building evidence of its effectiveness in improving social connectedness and health outcomes, as shown in a recently released evidence roundup from the Center for Health Care Strategies. However, more research is needed on how to implement effective social prescribing practices in the U.S. One such effort is a partnership between the Humana Foundation and the Aspen Institute to evaluate the prescribing, dosage and follow-up of relationship-building volunteer activities for diverse, underserved older adults who screen for loneliness or social isolation.

There is growing recognition of loneliness and social isolation as clinical risk factors impacting older adults’ health, independence and quality of life. Health professionals can play an essential role in identifying these risk factors and making social engagement a part of patients’ care looks. Support from health systems, philanthropy and the government is needed to staff and train teams, identify effective engagement strategies, build community partnerships, and establish pathways for referrals and follow-up. Working together, healthcare and community organizations can make social prescribing a practical component of age-friendly, whole-person care.

In a recent development, tiffany Benjamin is CEO of the Humana Foundation. Rani E. Snyder is President of The John A. Hartford Foundation.

Editor's note: The Humana Foundation provides support to The Aspen Institute. The John A. Hartford Foundation provides support to the American Library Association Aging Together initiative, the Social Prescribing USA Learning Hub, and the Center for Health Care Strategies' evidence roundup.

💡 Key Takeaways

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

An Oregon family transformed a mobile home that had sat abandoned for nearly five years into a home for a loved one–all without paying a dime for the property itself.

Industry observers note that but getting the home for free was only the beginning. What followed was months of demolition, electrical and plumbing work, drywall installation, and a race to get the aging property ready for its upcoming owner.

Lyman Branson II, who documented the transformation on I Can Fix That, his YouTube channel, took on the ambitious renovation alongside his family with one goal in mind: creating a safe, comfortable home for his sister, Betty Branson, 42, and her 17-year-old twin daughters.

Industry observers note that “I don't think I've ever had an opportunity like this before in my life, and so to turn it down would have been a shame,” Betty tells Realtor.com®. “And I know I would have regretted it, so this was probably one of the better decisions I've made in my life.”.

The family spent approximately $14,000 transforming the 1977 mobile home—a fraction of what Betty spent on rent in a year. Betty finally moved in the first week of May 2026, and now, just six months later, she is hosting her first Thanksgiving in the home her family helped bring back to life.

Lyman has worked in rental property maintenance and renovation since 2001, so he knew about the home in his small town of Irrigon, OR, that had been abandoned by the owner about five years earlier.

He discussed taking over the mobile home to renovate it and rent it out to someone in need. The landlord would be able to transfer the title to Lyman and later collect rent on the lot. Meanwhile, Lyman would be able to remove the property from the landlord’s possession.

“It was kind of like a ‘I scratch your back, you scratch my back’ kind of deal,” Branson tells Realtor.com.

It has been revealed that initially, Lyman saw the renovation as another project for his YouTube channel, which he released in early 2025. But the timing was also opportune for his sister, whose living circumstances had unexpectedly changed just days before he called.

Recent findings suggest that betty had been searching for another rental and considered buying an RV, paying approximately $800 a month for space at an RV park. Instead, her brother presented her with an opportunity to finally own a place of her own.

Betty could contribute what her brother calls “sweat equity,” working on the property before and after her regular job.

The purchase price was zero, but the property was far from move-in ready. The floors and walls were rotted, and there were leaks, water damage, and missing sections of ceiling.

“Basically, it was ready for the dump,” Lyman notes.

It has been revealed that with more than two decades of experience in the industry, he recognized that the structure was salvageable and the renovation worthwhile. Betty, however, was less convinced.

“I was a little overwhelmed and kind of scared when I first saw it,” she recalls.

She saw the home's many problems, including the broken countertop and the hole in the wall where a window would later be installed.

Recent findings suggest that the home remained in its original location, eliminating the expense of transporting it. However, it was still sitting on flat tires and had never been properly set up. So the family's first task was to stabilize the structure on blocks.

The landlord waived the lot rent for six months while the family obtained the necessary permits. Renovation began in October 2025. Lyman and his father, with help from other family members, updated the almost 50-year-old mobile home to current building codes.

They replaced broken flooring, added insulation and drywall, and wrapped the outside of the home to protect it from the elements. Lyman shared the process on his YouTube channel.

In a recent development, walls were painted, the bathroom drywall was finished, and the overall interior was beginning to look like a home. But the project wasn't without setbacks.

“There were a couple times that I was still in the middle of it all, and I'm like, 'We're too far in. I can't quit now,'” Betty recalls. “But this is hard and this is scary.”.

She had to depend on her brother and her father for help when various complications arose during the renovation.

“I'm so grateful because without them, this wouldn't have been possible for me,”  she notes.

Betty received her certificate of occupancy two weeks before the permit expired.

“I was actually really amazed that we were able to make it in the time frame that we did with how much that was done,” she notes.

The renovation offered Betty something she had never experienced in 20 years of renting. She got to design the layout of her living space. She got to pick out the locations of her light switches and outlets. Her daughters, who share a bedroom, chose paint colors and the arrangement for the closets.

“It was an experience for me that I'll never forget,” Betty says.

The renovation of the free mobile home came with substantial expenses.

It has been revealed that leAnna Branson, Lyman and Betty's mother, who kept track of the receipts for the renovation, tells Realtor.com that the family initially budgeted between $10,000 and $12,000. However, rising material costs, unexpected damage discovered during demolition, and decisions to upgrade certain features pushed the total to approximately $14,000.

Betty also opted to spend a little more on higher-quality materials and finishes, knowing she intended to live there for years.

Recent findings suggest that “I could have gone cheaper. Definitely, we could have cut some costs here and there,” she says. “But I strategy to be here for a while. I want it to last.”.

Betty used her savings to kick-start the renovation and lived in her sister’s RV, which allowed her to devote her income to the renovation for six months. Once she moved in and began paying rent on the lot, plus utilities, the pace of the work slowed a bit.

According to recent reports, now, Lyman estimates the renovation is approximately 90% complete. The remaining work involves the upper kitchen cabinets, wall tile, a window replacement, and several finishing touches.

It has been revealed that the family also received support from viewers of Lyman's YouTube channel, who contributed an estimated $1,000 to $2,000. Even the handles that will adorn Betty's kitchen cabinets and drawers were paid for by a viewer.

“More support than I ever imagined,” Lyman claims of the response to the project. His viewers “loved seeing the family aspect.”.

For Betty, the financial benefits extend well beyond the renovation costs. She claims she has more living space than she would have gotten in an apartment. And there's space for her daughters and her dog.

According to recent reports, “We went over budget a little, but considering [Betty] was paying $20,000 a year to rent, $14,000 is not that bad,” LeAnna indicates. “I mean it's a chunk of money, but it's doable.”.

Lyman believes owning a mobile home, even when you must rent the land it sits on, can offer an affordable housing alternative to people struggling to keep up with rising rental costs across the country.

“That was key for Betty as well, so that she could afford to live the life she deserves,” he indicates.

Though Betty’s experience highlights that acquiring a free or inexpensive mobile home is only a small part of the financial equation, her brother’s professional experience, the family’s help, and the landlord’s willingness to waive her lot rent during the renovation also helped keep costs manageable.

For her parents, seeing their daughter choose everything from her kitchen sink to her bathroom tile was particularly rewarding.

“It gave us a peace of mind to know, you know, that she finally has a place of her own to call her home,” her mother says.

Some of the most special features of her newly introduced home are things visitors won’t see. Behind her new cupboards are messages from her family who helped her renovate her home.

Recent findings suggest that “I have places on the wall behind some of the cupboards where the family all, like, signed their names and left me love notes,” Betty notes. “I know they're there, even though some of them are covered up.”.

The transformation is a daily reminder of what her family made possible.

According to recent reports, “The fact that it was my family that assisted me along the way makes it even more special,” she says. “It wasn't just hiring outside help, but family and friends that came to put in the time and effort that they could to help. It makes it mean so much more to me.”.

UPDATED 16:12 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Lawmakers on both sides of the aisle are criticizing Nvidia Corp.’s decision to rehire Jensen Huang as its chief executive.

The criticism came against the backdrop of a controversial move by the U.S. Commerce Department. The agency applied new export restrictions to Megaspeed, a Singapore-based cloud operator. The company played a prominent role in the spy controversy that led to Huang’s resignation. According to trade experts, the Commerce Department left out a key clause that is usually included in such restrictions.

Huang resigned on Nov. 12 following revelations that he had an affair with Alice Huang, a former Megaspeed executive. Early reporting about the relationship indicated that she was found to have passed intelligence to China. The U.S. Justice Department later stated that it has not yet reached a conclusion on whether Alice Huang is a spy. Earlier this week, the New York Times reported that she maintained contact with a Chinese intelligence official.

Nvidia’s board reinstated Jensen Huang on Monday after U.S. President Donald Trump and tech industry figures urged directors to bring him back. The move drew widespread criticism from members of Congress.

House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries (D-Fresh York), who is set to become House Speaker, called the reinstatement “indefensible, irresponsible and incomprehensible.” Rep. Don Bacon (R-Nebraska), the chair of House Subcommittee on Cyber, Information Technologies and Innovation, stated that “it’s inexplicable to me why they want this guy back as CEO.” Former Utah Republican Senator and Massachusetts Governor Mitt Romney tweeted: “Let me get this straight: we rushed AI along without regulating safeguards in order to stay ahead of China and at the same time, we sold China the very chips they’d need to get ahead of us. Smells of profit, corruption and perhaps worse.”.

Recent findings suggest that multiple lawmakers told CNBC that they strategy to scrutinize Huang’s conduct closely. The executive is scheduled to testify before multiple Congressional committees next Tuesday. Furthermore, Sen. Ron Wyden (D-Oregon) told the outlet that Democrats plan to scrutinize the Trump administration’s role in the matter.

The Commerce Department today added Megaspeed and several of its regional affiliates to its Entity List. Companies on the list can only purchase sensitive products such as graphics cards if they obtain a license from the U.S. government. According to Gizmodo, the move has drawn scrutiny because the restrictions applied to Megaspeed include a loophole.

All the companies on the Entity List are prohibited from buying Nvidia’s latest chips unless they secure a license. Most of them are also unable to buy lower-end graphics cards, high-bandwidth memory and related hardware. The latter restrictions are specified in a clause called the FDPR provision. The Commerce Department has reportedly not applied the FDPR provision to Megaspeed when it added the manufacturer to the Entity List.

In a recent development, huang returned to Nvidia’s Santa Clara headquarters on Monday. The news sent the chipmaker’s stock soaring more than 30%, although it parred some of the gains today. Nvidia shares are down 5.8% from Monday.

Wired today published excerpts from Huang’s all-hands meeting with employees. The executive apologized for his affairs and for his management style, which has also come under scrutiny in recent days. He added that he will undergo a “360-degree review” and that Nvidia’s code of conduct is still in effect.

Latest Update: New wearable ultrasound patch boosts REM sleep without drugs or surgery

📅 16 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1028 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A upcoming wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most notable stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery.
  • Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time.
  • Recent findings suggest that REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A upcoming wearable patch could offer a surprisingly simple way to improve one of the most notable stages of sleep, without relying on medication or surgery. Developed by researchers led by the University of Texas at Austin, the device uses gentle ultrasound waves to stimulate regions deep inside the brain, helping people enter REM sleep sooner and spend more time in this restorative stage.

Known as NEUSLeeP, the soft patch attaches to the skin and combines ultrasound stimulation with electrodes that monitor brain activity in real time. This allows researchers to influence brain regions involved in sleep while simultaneously tracking how the brain responds.

Recent findings suggest that REM sleep, short for rapid eye movement sleep, is the stage when most vivid dreaming occurs. It also plays an important role in processing emotions, consolidating memories, and adapting to stress. Disturbances in this stage of sleep have been associated with several mental health conditions, making it an important target for new treatments.

Recent findings suggest that "This is the first time we've been able to noninvasively target deep brain regions involved in REM sleep, while simultaneously monitoring brain activity," noted Kai Wing "Kevin" Tang, a recent UT biomedical engineering Ph.D. graduate who led the research effort.

"Our skin-attached NEUSLeeP patch opens up newly introduced possibilities for understanding sleep and treating sleep disorders in home settings," added Huiliang "Evan" Wang, assistant professor in the Cockrell School of Engineering's Department of Biomedical Engineering. Wang supervised Tang's research and served as the principal investigator (PI) overseeing the project.

Sleep Patch Helps People Reach REM Sleep 43 Minutes Faster.

The early results suggest that the technology can make a measurable difference in how people experience REM sleep.

In a study involving 28 participants, published in Nature Communications, people using the patch entered REM sleep an average of 43 minutes sooner and spent approximately 16 additional minutes in that stage.

These improvements were observed in both healthy sleepers and participants experiencing certain sleep difficulties. The volunteers also reported that the patch was comfortable to wear, with minimal adverse effects.

Recent findings suggest that unlike medications that affect the body more broadly, NEUSLeeP is designed to deliver stimulation to specific brain regions involved in sleep regulation. It uses ultrasound, a form of sound energy with frequencies beyond human hearing, to reach areas beneath the surface of the brain without requiring an invasive procedure.

The findings are encouraging, although the relatively small study means that larger trials will be needed to determine how consistently the technology works and whether its benefits persist over time.

Potential Benefits for Stress and Emotional Health.

The researchers also found evidence that the patch's effects may extend beyond increasing REM sleep.

Sources indicate that among healthy participants, ultrasound stimulation improved heart rate variability, a measure of the natural differences in time between consecutive heartbeats. This measurement provides insight into how the body's nervous system responds to stress and adjusts to changing conditions.

Brain imaging revealed changes in neural circuits involved in emotional processing. Together, these findings suggest that improving REM sleep through targeted stimulation could potentially support emotional regulation and the ability to cope with stress.

In a recent development, "REM sleep is not just about dreaming -- it's about emotional reset and stress adaptation," explained Gregory Fonzo, assistant professor in the Dell Medical School's Department of Psychiatry and Behavioral Sciences and one of the project's co-PIs. "By enhancing REM, we may help people better cope with stress and improve their overall well-being.".

These possibilities are especially interesting because REM sleep disturbances have been linked to depression, anxiety, and post-traumatic stress disorder (PTSD).

According to recent reports, current approaches to sleep problems often involve medication or behavioral therapy. Although these treatments can be effective, medications may produce unwanted side effects, and existing approaches do not always directly address the biological processes responsible for disrupted REM sleep.

A device capable of influencing those processes without drugs or surgery could therefore offer an additional treatment option. However, the researchers have not yet established whether NEUSLeeP can improve symptoms of mental health disorders.

A New Direction for Treating Insomnia and PTSD.

Building on the initial findings, the research team intends to conduct larger clinical trials to confirm the patch's effects and investigate its potential use in people with PTSD, depression, and chronic insomnia.

Beyond treating sleep disorders, the technology could eventually support sleep monitoring at home and provide scientists with a latest way to study how deep brain regions influence sleep. Researchers also envision personalized therapies that could be adjusted to individual sleep patterns and needs.

In a recent development, "Our vision is a future where patients with mental health disorders can optimize their sleep with a noninvasive and safe treatment," mentioned Vincent Mysliwiec, M.D., a professor at UT Health San Antonio, a leading expert in sleep disorders, and another co-PI on the project. "This technology could help millions of people get the restorative sleep they need.".

The team is already taking steps toward making NEUSLeeP available beyond the research setting. Working with the university's commercialization unit, Discovery to Impact, the researchers are exploring how to bring the device to market and have filed a patent application covering the technology.

If future studies confirm the early results, this wearable ultrasound patch could become a valuable new tool for improving REM sleep and potentially addressing conditions associated with poor sleep.

Recent findings suggest that other members of the research team include William D. Moscoso-Barrera, Mengxia Yu, Mengmeng Yao, Jinmo Jeong, Ilya Pyatnitskiy, Anakaren Romero Lozano, Jiachen Wang, Ju-Chun Hsieh, Tony Sungjin Chae, Daniel Song, Julieta Garcia, Rithvik Mittapalli, and Adam Bush of the Department of Biomedical Engineering; Benjamin Baird of the College of Natural Sciences' Department of Psychology; and Wynn Legon of Virginia Tech's Fralin Biomedical Research Institute.

#156716. Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 7m • 📚 Deep Dive (1480 w)
📖 Baca
General 📈 Bullish 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

Wine, beer, or spirits? Massive study reveals a surprising health divide

📅 17 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 7 min read (1480 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~7 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits.
  • According to recent reports, researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease.
  • According to recent reports, the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that A massive study involving more than 340,000 adults has uncovered a surprising difference in the health risks associated with wine, beer, cider, and spirits. Although heavy drinking was linked to worse health outcomes regardless of the beverage, the picture was more complicated among people who consumed smaller amounts of alcohol.

According to recent reports, researchers found that low to moderate wine consumption was associated with a lower risk of death, particularly from cardiovascular disease. In contrast, similar amounts of beer, cider, and spirits were linked to a higher risk. The findings, presented at the American College of Cardiology's Annual Scientific Session (ACC.26), suggest that both the type and quantity of alcohol may influence its relationship with long-term health.

According to recent reports, the results also reinforce a broader conclusion from previous research: drinking less alcohol is generally better for health. Importantly, the latest findings do not establish that wine itself protects against disease.

"These results come from the general population, and in certain high-risk groups, such as people with chronic diseases or cardiovascular conditions, the risks could be even higher," said Zhangling Chen, MD, PhD, a professor at the Second Xiangya Hospital, Central South University in China and the study's senior author.

How a Study of 340,000 Adults Measured Alcohol Risk.

Industry observers note that to investigate the relationship between drinking habits and longevity, scientists examined data from 340,924 adults enrolled in the UK Biobank between 2006 and 2022. The UK Biobank is a large research resource that collects health and lifestyle information to help scientists investigate factors associated with disease and mortality.

Participants reported their alcohol consumption through dietary questionnaires when they joined the study. Researchers then classified them into four groups based on how much pure alcohol they typically consumed each day or week, rather than simply counting drinks.

Industry observers note that this distinction matters because beer, wine, and spirits contain different concentrations of alcohol. For comparison, a 12-ounce can of beer, a 5-ounce glass of wine, and a 1.5-ounce shot of spirits each provide approximately 14 grams of pure alcohol.

People consuming fewer than 20 g (about 1.5 standard drinks) per week were placed in the never or occasional drinking group. Low consumption was defined as 20 g per week up to 20 g per day for men, and 20 g per week up to 10 g per day for women.

In a recent development, moderate drinking was defined as 20 g to 40 g (about 1.5 to three standard drinks) daily for men and 10 g to 20 g daily for women. High consumption meant more than 40 g (about three drinks) per day for men or more than 20 g (about 1.5 drinks) per day for women.

Researchers followed participants' health outcomes for an average of more than 13 years, allowing them to examine how drinking patterns were associated with deaths from different causes.

Wine, Beer, and Spirits Show Different Heart Health Risks.

The clearest finding concerned heavy alcohol consumption. Compared with people who never drank or consumed alcohol only occasionally, heavy drinkers had a 24% higher risk of dying from any cause. Their risk of dying from cancer was 36% higher, while their risk of dying from heart disease was 14% higher.

These increased risks were associated with heavy drinking regardless of whether participants preferred wine, beer, cider, or spirits.

Recent findings suggest that however, the results became more surprising when researchers examined low and moderate alcohol consumption. At these levels, the type of beverage was associated with substantially different outcomes.

People who consumed wine in low to moderate amounts had a significantly lower risk of death, while those who consumed comparable amounts of beer, cider, or spirits had a significantly higher risk.

Sources indicate that the contrast was especially striking for cardiovascular disease, a broad category of conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels. Moderate wine drinkers had a 21% lower risk of dying from cardiovascular disease than people who never or only occasionally drank alcohol.

By comparison, even low consumption of beer, cider, or spirits was associated with a 9% higher risk of cardiovascular death.

These percentages describe relative differences in risk between groups, not the absolute probability that an individual will die from cardiovascular disease. Because the research was observational, the findings also cannot demonstrate that choosing one alcoholic beverage over another directly changes a person's risk.

Industry observers note that "Our findings help clarify previously mixed evidence on low to moderate alcohol consumption," Chen stated. "These findings can help refine guidance, emphasizing that the health risks of alcohol depend not only on the amount of alcohol consumed, but also on the type of beverage. Even low to moderate intake of spirits, beer, or cider is linked to higher mortality, while low to moderate intake of wine may carry lower risk.".

Why Might Wine Be Linked to Lower Heart Risks?

Researchers identified several possible explanations for the differences, including the chemical composition of wine and the habits of people who drink it.

Red wine contains polyphenols, naturally occurring compounds found in plants that can have antioxidant properties. Antioxidants help counter certain chemical reactions involving unstable molecules that can damage cells. Some polyphenols have been investigated for potential benefits to blood vessels and cardiovascular function.

These compounds could contribute to the associations observed in wine drinkers, although the study did not establish that they were responsible for the lower mortality risk.

Another possible explanation involves how and when people drink.

Recent findings suggest that wine is more commonly consumed alongside meals, and wine drinkers often report healthier diets and lifestyle habits. Drinking wine may therefore be associated with other behaviors that support cardiovascular health.

Beer, cider, and spirits, on the other hand, are more frequently consumed outside of meals. In this study, people who favored these beverages also tended to have poorer overall diet quality and other lifestyle factors associated with increased health risks.

Such differences make it difficult to separate the effects of the alcohol itself from the characteristics and habits of the people consuming it.

"Taken together, these factors suggest that the type of alcohol, how it is consumed, and the associated lifestyle behaviors all contribute to the observed differences in mortality risk," Chen noted.

What the Findings Mean for Alcohol and Health.

To make their comparisons more reliable, the researchers statistically adjusted their analyses for numerous factors that might influence mortality. These included age and other demographic characteristics, socioeconomic circumstances, lifestyle behaviors, and cardiometabolic health.

Industry observers note that cardiometabolic factors include conditions and measurements related to heart and metabolic health, such as blood pressure, blood sugar regulation, and cholesterol levels. The analyses also accounted for family histories of diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and cancer.

Even with these adjustments, the researchers emphasized several vital limitations.

Because the study was observational, it could identify associations between alcohol consumption and mortality but could not prove that particular beverages caused better or worse outcomes. Other differences between participants may have influenced the findings despite the statistical adjustments.

According to recent reports, alcohol intake was also measured through questionnaires completed when participants first entered the study. That information depended on participants accurately reporting their own drinking habits, and it did not capture changes in consumption during the years that followed.

Another consideration is that UK Biobank participants tend to be healthier than the general population. This could limit how well the findings apply to other groups of people.

The researchers suggested that high-quality randomized trials could provide stronger evidence about the health effects of different drinking patterns. Such studies would help clarify whether the observed differences reflect the beverages themselves or other factors associated with their consumption.

Nevertheless, the enormous study population and more than 13 years of average follow-up provide considerable statistical strength. By examining specific types of alcohol, different levels of consumption, and multiple causes of death, the research offers a more detailed picture of alcohol's potential health risks than many earlier investigations.

The findings highlight an crucial distinction: while heavy drinking is consistently associated with harmful health outcomes, the relationships observed at lower consumption levels may depend on beverage choice, drinking habits, and broader lifestyle patterns.

In a recent development, for now, the apparent advantage among wine drinkers should not be interpreted as a reason to start drinking wine for heart health. The evidence points to a complex relationship between alcohol and mortality, rather than proving that any alcoholic drink offers protection.

Ziyue Li presented the study, "Alcohol Use at Mid-Life and All-Cause and Cause-Specific Mortality," at ACC.26.

How messaging could be the next source of clinician burnout" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Physician burnout may be falling nationally, but healthcare leaders are noting a potential fresh source of overwhelm: messaging overload.

And, it’s not affecting all providers equally.

Leaders at Ochsner Health, per the American Medical Association (AMA), found female physicians receive about 30% more staff messages and 30% more patient messages than their male counterparts through an analysis of electronic health record (EHR) data.

Though the direct causes are unknown, TigerConnect Chief Growth Officer Sheeza Hussain noted general messaging overload is a “symptom of a coordination problem.”.

“Healthcare slows down when people are waiting for information, decisions, consults, transfers, and discharges and all the handoffs in between,” Hussain mentioned. “At TigerConnect, we focus on helping health systems remove those bottlenecks by connecting people, systems and workflows so communication moves care forward.”.

Hussain continued, “When communication is orchestrated well, clinicians can focus on care, and patients can move through their care journey more smoothly and effectively.”.

Hussain and Nikki Manuel, TigerConnect clinical solution design director, spoke with Fierce Healthcare about the factors driving this trend, impacts on patient experience and how health systems can mitigate it.

Editor’s note: The following Q&A has been edited for length and clarity.

Fierce Healthcare: Why does message overload land unevenly in hospitals and health systems?

Nikki Manuel: Nurses are at the center of patient care and care coordination, so a significant share of the communication burden often falls on them. Think about a nurse trying to reach the right provider about a change in a patient’s condition. They may need to review the EHR, confirm who is on call, determine the preferred communication method and follow up if there is no response—all while managing other patients. The burden grows when communication crosses departments or shifts and ownership is unclear. The clinicians coordinating those handoffs can end up spending valuable time navigating the communication process instead of moving more rapidly to the next step in care.

In a recent development, sheeza Hussain: In my conversations with health system leaders, it comes back to fragmentation. Healthcare has never lacked technology, but more technology hasn’t created more connected care. Hospitals run single-purpose communication tools, fleets of devices, and disconnected biomedical equipment, putting out huge volumes of alerts and alarms. None of it coordinates, which puts clinicians in the role of middleware. It’s not a tool shortage. It’s a coordination problem.

FH: As this trend takes shape, who are the clinicians most affected by potential overload?

Sources indicate that hussain: Nurses, first. They’re asked to manually bridge disconnected systems and respond to alarms. Most alarms don’t need a response, but a nurse still has to hear every one to find out. Hospitalists and on-call physicians feel it too, especially when coverage isn’t clear. Clinicians should not be middleware.

FH: How, if at all, is messaging overload shaping up to be the next source of burnout for clinicians?

Manuel: I don’t think messaging itself is necessarily the next source of burnout. In many ways, messaging has made communication easier. As a bedside nurse, I remember relying on pagers and phone calls and having to stop what I was doing when a provider called back. Messaging gives clinicians more flexibility to communicate without constantly interrupting patient care.

It has been revealed that the burden comes when we layer messaging onto communication processes that haven’t been standardized. Nurses are already surrounded by alerts, messages, and notifications coming from multiple systems, and they’re often the ones deciding what needs action, who needs to receive it, and what to do when there isn’t a response. That’s where the cognitive load starts to build.

In a recent development, health systems should be looking at where communication can be standardized and where alerts, routing and escalation can be automated. Technology should support that process by identifying the appropriate person and helping get the right information to them without requiring a nurse to manually connect every step. Nurses shouldn’t have to serve as the middleware holding the communication process together.

Sources indicate that hussain: Because it adds to a load clinicians already carry. They’re surrounded by beeps, pings, messages and alerts, and most of it does not need action. The requirement to still read these messages and make that decision adds to cognitive overload and burnout.

It’s a thousand small interruptions compounded by the need to choose which tool to use to communicate. And the risk goes beyond burnout. When people tune out the noise, a real emergency can slip past. That’s a patient safety issue.

FH: Why do some organizations not have clear communication rules?

Manuel: Communication practices often evolve over time as organizations grow, add upcoming technology and adapt workflows across different departments and care teams. That can naturally lead to different ways of communicating depending on the team, the workflow or even the situation. The important thing is establishing clear communication standards and governance around those practices.

In a recent development, hussain: Many hospitals do not have clear communication rules because communication has evolved department by department and tool by tool, rather than as an enterprise-wide workflow strategy. Health systems have invested in a lot of technology, but more technology has not always translated into more coordinated care. The result is that a nurse, physician or operator may have to decide which system to use, who to contact, how urgent the issue is and what to do if there is no response. That is a lot of operational burden being pushed onto clinicians.

Clear communication rules are important, but they also have to be supported by technology that can operationalize those rules in real time.

Sources indicate that FH: As messaging providers has become more commonplace at health systems, some have begun to charge for the service. How has that impacted overload, if at all?

Manuel: Research has shown that charging for certain patient messages can reduce message volume, but I don’t think we can assume that fewer messages automatically translates to less burden for clinicians.

We also have to consider the potential impact on patient access. We don’t want patients hesitating to reach out with questions or concerns because they’re unsure whether they’ll be charged. From a clinical perspective, the bigger question is whether we’re reducing the work associated with managing communication. If clinicians are still sorting through unnecessary messages, tracking down information or following up on requests that weren’t routed appropriately, we haven’t really addressed the underlying burden.

Charging may influence volume, but improving how communication is managed is what can make a meaningful difference.

FH: How does message overload ultimately affect patient experience and engagement?

In a recent development, manuel: When we talk about message overload, I think the impact on patients is really about whether communication is helping care move forward or creating additional work and delays. When information is clear, actionable, and reaches the right person at the right time, clinicians can make decisions faster, reduce unnecessary delays, and keep care moving forward. When communication becomes fragmented or creates unnecessary noise, it can have the opposite effect.

Communication is also an important part of patient engagement. Patients want to understand what’s happening with their care, have their questions answered, and feel involved in decisions. When communication processes work well, clinicians have more time for those meaningful interactions and to apply their clinical judgment where it’s needed most. There’s also an element of confidence and trust. Patients may not see all of the communication happening behind the scenes, but they experience the result of it. When the care team is aligned, information is consistent, and next steps are clear, patients have greater confidence in their care and a better understanding of what to expect.

FH: How can leadership change communication without disrupting patient care?

Industry observers note that hussain: Leadership can start by treating communication as a patient-care-affecting workflow, not just a technology or etiquette opportunity. The goal is not to slow communication down or create more rules for clinicians to remember. The goal is to make communication more reliable so [that] the right information reaches the right person with the right level of urgency. That requires involving frontline clinicians, understanding where delays and interruptions are happening, and then standardizing the workflows that create the most friction. Done well, this should reduce disruption because clinicians are no longer forced to manually manage every handoff, escalation, or follow-up themselves.

FH: More broadly, what can hospitals and health systems do to mitigate this overload?

Hussain: Hospitals and health systems need to look at overload as a coordination problem. Clinicians are receiving messages, alerts, alarms and requests from many different systems, but those systems often are not working together. The first step is understanding where volume is coming from and which communications are truly actionable. From there, organizations can clarify escalation paths, reduce duplicative tools, and route communication based on role, schedule, urgency and context. Technology can help, but only if it is designed around the workflow.

FH: How could AI or other kinds of health tech provide relief for clinicians?

Hussain: AI and health tech can provide relief when they are built into real clinical workflows, not layered on top of them as another tool to manage. Clinicians do not need more alerts, inboxes or systems to check. They need technology that can reduce noise, understand urgency, identify the right person, and help activate the next step without forcing nurses, physicians or operators to manually coordinate it all.

It has been revealed that this is where communication orchestration matters. The goal, and much of the work we focus on at TigerConnect, is to help health systems move from fragmented communication to smarter, role-based workflows that reach the right person at the right time. Used well, AI can help filter low-value communication, route information more precisely and automate routine coordination so clinicians can spend less time managing the work around care and more time with patients.

Industry observers note that for the quarter that ended on Oct. 31, Workday reported adjusted earnings per share of $2.82, up 22% from $2.32 in the same quarter of the previous year, on revenue of $2.705 billion, up 11.2% year-over-year. Analysts were expecting earnings of $2.75 per share on revenue of $2.69 billion.

Subscription revenue rose 12.8% from a year earlier, to $2.532 billion. Net income on an unadjusted basis came to $237 million, down from $252 million in the same quarter a year ago. Included in the quarter were $51 million in restructuring expenses, which followed the organization’s disclosure in late September that it would cut about 2.5% of its workforce, mostly in its product and technology team.

Industry observers note that total subscription revenue backlog grew 6.1%, to $27.548 billion, with the 12-month figure up 12.3%, to $9.216 billion. Free cash flow came to $691 million, up from $550 million. During the quarter, Workday spent $750 million buying back about 3.8 million shares.

Industry observers note that the quarter also saw Workday hold its annual Rising customer conference in Las Vegas in October, when the tech giant made Sana the fresh home experience for its platform. Built on technology from Sana Labs AB, which Workday acquired for about $1.1 billion last year, Sana is an AI interface that brings tasks, decisions, meetings and agent activity together in one place. Autopilot Agents, also released at the event, are designed to handle routine HR, finance and IT processes in the background.

Industry observers note that on the opening day of Rising, Workday confirmed that it had agreed to acquire agentic identity platform ConductorOne Inc., better known as C1.ai. That deal closed on Monday. A partnership with Anthropic PBC, also unveiled at Rising, is set to bring Claude together with Sana AI agents and Workday’s HR and finance data.

It has been revealed that “The past few quarters have been our strongest on the innovation and invention front, and in Q3, our AI products drove nearly $150 million in new ACV, more than three times what we delivered a year ago,” stated co-founder and Chief Executive Aneel Bhusri, who returned to the top job in February after Carl Eschenbach stepped down. The priority now, Bhusri added, is to get more customers running agents in production.

According to Workday, the number of core customers that have bought at least one of its AI products rose nearly 25% from the previous quarter, to more than 2,200.

Pointing to what he called “ongoing adoption across our AI portfolio,” Chief Financial Officer Zane Rowe stated the organization is raising its full-year targets.

Industry observers note that for its fiscal fourth quarter, Workday expects subscription revenue of $2.6 billion, up 10%, and an adjusted operating margin of 31.7%. Full-year subscription revenue is now forecast at $9.958 billion, up 13%, compared with the $9.94 billion to $9.95 billion guided in August. The full-year adjusted operating margin forecast was also raised, to 31.5%, ahead of the 31.1% expected by analysts.

According to recent reports, though the full-year numbers moved higher, the fourth-quarter subscription forecast came in narrowly below the $2.61 billion analysts had been expecting. Growth of 10% in the period would also be a step down from the 12.8% Workday posted in the third quarter.

Industry News: Cannabis addiction linked to 57% higher odds of suicidal thoughts

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health.
  • Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition.
  • In a recent development, the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

As marijuana becomes more widely available and accepted, researchers are uncovering important questions about its effects on mental health. A major new study suggests that people who struggle to control their cannabis use face a substantially greater likelihood of experiencing suicidal thoughts.

Published in the Journal of Studies on Alcohol and Drugs, the research found that adults with cannabis use disorder had 57% higher odds of reporting suicidal thoughts compared with those without the condition. Despite major shifts in marijuana laws and public attitudes, this troubling association remained remarkably consistent over a decade.

In a recent development, the findings come from an analysis of more than 415,000 American adults who participated in the National Survey on Drug Use and Health. Researchers examined data collected between 2014 and 2023, a period when cannabis became increasingly accessible across the United States.

Recent findings suggest that "What surprised me most was not that cannabis use disorder was associated with suicidal thoughts, but that this association did not appear to strengthen over time," stated lead author Tosin Philip Oyetunji, MPH, a doctoral student in public health at the University of California, Merced. "[Yet,] it remains an important mental health concern that deserves attention.".

Cannabis and Suicidal Thoughts Show a Persistent Link.

The connection between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thinking was observed across different age groups, sexes, and racial and ethnic backgrounds. However, women and younger adults highlighted particularly elevated risks.

Importantly, the association remained even after researchers accounted for depression, psychological distress, and other factors that could influence mental health outcomes.

According to recent reports, the consistency of the results was especially notable given how dramatically the cannabis landscape has changed. Recreational marijuana is now legal in half of U.S. states, and cannabis products have become increasingly potent. These developments have raised concerns among public health experts about whether broader access might contribute to worsening mental health.

Recent findings suggest that yet the study offers some reassurance on that particular question. Sidra Goldman-Mellor, PhD, a professor of public health at UC Merced and the study's senior author, noted that the association between cannabis use disorder and suicidal thoughts did not become stronger during the 10 years examined.

"Suicidal ideation does not seem to have increased among people with cannabis use disorder, despite all this legal and social change," explained Goldman-Mellor. Yet, "people with cannabis use disorder are still at a very substantially increased likelihood of experiencing serious suicidal thoughts, and that's not something that is widely understood.".

Why Cannabis Use Disorder Matters.

The researchers stress that these findings should not be interpreted as evidence that everyone who uses marijuana faces the same elevated risk.

The study focused specifically on cannabis use disorder, a condition in which people have difficulty controlling their marijuana consumption even when it causes problems in their lives. Someone with the disorder may continue using cannabis despite harmful consequences or repeated attempts to cut back.

This distinction is notable because problematic cannabis use differs from occasional or otherwise nonproblematic consumption.

Sources indicate that the findings also do not establish that cannabis use disorder directly causes suicidal thoughts. Because the research identified an association rather than a cause-and-effect relationship, it cannot determine whether problematic cannabis use contributes to suicidal thinking, whether underlying mental health difficulties contribute to both conditions, or whether other factors help explain the connection.

Nevertheless, the results point to a significant mental health concern that deserves greater recognition, particularly among people seeking help for problematic cannabis use.

Researchers Urge Greater Mental Health Screening.

One practical implication is that health care professionals should look beyond cannabis consumption itself when evaluating patients with cannabis use disorder.

Recent findings suggest that rather than focusing exclusively on depression or substance use symptoms, clinicians may benefit from asking patients directly about suicidal thoughts as part of a broader mental health assessment. This could help identify people who need additional care but whose struggles might otherwise remain unnoticed.

In a recent development, "Someone seeking help for cannabis use disorder may also be experiencing suicidal thoughts that are not immediately apparent," noted Oyetunji. "The goal is not to assume that everyone with cannabis use disorder is suicidal but to identify those who may need additional assessment, treatment, or support.".

Recent findings suggest that the study arrives at a time when marijuana is increasingly viewed as a relatively low-risk substance. Public perceptions have shifted considerably, and negative attitudes toward cannabis have declined alongside expanding legalization and social acceptance.

However, these changes have not eliminated the mental health challenges associated with cannabis use disorder. Even though the strength of the association with suicidal thoughts did not increase over the study period, the elevated odds remained substantial.

The researchers suggest that health care providers, policymakers, and community organizations can play an vital role by improving awareness, identifying vulnerable individuals, and making appropriate mental health support more accessible.

As attitudes toward marijuana continue to evolve, the findings serve as a reminder that the needs of people experiencing problematic cannabis use should remain a public health priority.

Stated Oyetunji, "As cannabis becomes more accessible and socially accepted, we should ensure that the people struggling with its use are not overlooked.".

Court strikes down anti-trans Ryan White funding rules 'based in animus, loathing and discrimination'" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Medical associations and providers notched a legal victory over the federal government in a court ruling vacating federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

Those restrictions would have required recipients of Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care.

It was challenged by the HIV Medicine Association of the Infectious Diseases Society of America (HIVMA), the American Academy of HIV Medicine and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care in June (see that coverage below), who argued that the policy was contrary to Congress' intent when establishing the program under law in 1991, lacked sufficient explanation and discriminated against transgender people in violation of the First and Fifth Amendments.

Industry observers note that the Nov. 19 decision from Judge William G. Young, of the U.S. District Court for the District of Massachusetts, prohibits the government from opposing its conditions in regard to all federal funding and permanently blocks any similar policies from being implemented by associational plaintifs' members, "which covers virtually every HIV care provider in the United States," remarked Lambda Legal, which acted as co-counsel for the plaintiffs.

"The ruling is a decisive and crucial victory for transgender people with HIV and protects the ability of physicians and other health care professionals to offer evidence-based care without political interference," Philip Bolduc, M.D., chair of HIVMA, noted in a statement reacting to the decision.

Young's opinion and order opened with an acknowledgement that there are "sincere and deeply felt views" regarding transgender identity, and that the matter at question was of legal regulation rather than "the propriety of individual gender expression.".

Still, the judge concluded his opinion by writing that the administration's conditions "are based in animus, loathing and discrimination. They do not stand for justice—in fact, they defy it. They are contrary to the laws of this nation and cannot continue to stand.".

A group of medical associations and providers has filed a lawsuit challenging fresh federal funding requirements for Ryan White clinics involving gender-affirming care.

The new requirements, issued in a recent HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity, require recipients of the Ryan White HIV/AIDS Program funds to not acknowledge the identities of transgender patients or use funds for gender-affirming care. The restrictions undermine the very intent of the program, the plaintiffs say, and violate anti-discrimination components of the Fifth Amendment.

Sources indicate that “The Ryan White Program was created as a public health intervention to address the needs of low-income, vulnerable populations who otherwise would not have access to life-saving care,” Melanie Thompson, M.D., co-chair of a primary care guidance panel for the HIV Medicine Association, noted in a press release. “It is crucial that Ryan White clinicians be allowed to continue to deliver the most scientifically appropriate treatments for all patients, including transgender individuals, without discrimination if we are to improve health outcomes for all and end the U.S. HIV epidemic.".

The lawsuit alleges (PDF) that HHS and HRSA violated the Administrative Procedure Act by exceeding their statutory authority and imposing restrictions that conflict with the Ryan White statute. The plaintiffs ask the court to block enforcement of the funding restrictions.

The case was filed by Lambda Legal and HSF Kramer on behalf of the American Academy of HIV Medicine, the HIV Medicine Association and the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care, plus two providers.

A preliminary hearing will likely be scheduled in a few weeks. Lambda Legal is “cautiously optimistic” about the future of the case, José Abrigo, senior attorney and HIV project director at Lambda Legal, told reporters on a webinar on Thursday afternoon. He called the administration’s actions “unlawful,” and said gender-affirming care in this context includes all types of care, including primary care and mental healthcare.

Specifically, the HRSA Notice of Funding Opportunity reads: “Discretionary awards shall not be used to fund, promote, encourage, subsidize, or facilitate … denial by the recipient of the sex binary in humans, or the belief that sex is a chosen or mutable characteristic.”.

In a recent development, some providers are already preemptively complying with the restrictions, Abrigo noted, particularly in Tennessee and Kentucky. It is unclear how many other providers will also stop gender-affirming care. In certain cases, it’s up to individual states or departments of health to enforce the restrictions. It’s possible that medical records could be audited and reviewed for indications of pronouns, per Thompson. “It does matter what someone’s gender and pronouns are listed as,” Thompson said on the webinar, explaining that medical records are shared between providers and help ensure affirming care.

It has been revealed that if a clinic is found to be non-compliant, the repercussions are steep, Thompson added. “The penalty for being found out is severe, and puts an entire program’s funding in jeopardy,” she stated on the webinar.

Forty percent of American Academy of HIV Medicine members rely on Ryan White funding, of which 40% voluntarily report providing gender-affirming medical care. For low-income trans individuals with HIV, there aren’t many alternative options, per Abrigo. They may seek care through private insurance or potentially through Medicaid, but typically the population relies on Ryan White clinics for services.

Gender-affirming care restrictions under the Trump administration have been commonplace. Over 40 hospitals have reportedly stopped some gender-affirming care services for minors in response to pressure. Last week, the Cleveland Clinic promised the Department of Justice (DOJ) to commit $2 million to detransitioning services and a “decades-long” agreement not to perform gender-affirming care on minors. Delivering most of these services is currently illegal for minors under Ohio state law. Last month, DOJ struck a similar deal with Texas Children’s.

It has been revealed that for months, experts have been sounding the alarm about the U.S. HIV response slipping into dangerous instability. In April, the International Association of Providers of AIDS Care (IAPAC) released a data brief finding that 61% of providers have reported at least one HIV service disruption and 68% have seen operational changes such as staffing reductions, service cutbacks and program closures. This was attributed to a combination of policy decisions, funding cuts and social determinants like loss of insurance coverage.

According to recent reports, “It’s a catastrophe in the making," José M. Zúñiga, AIPAC's president and CEO, told reporters on the webinar. "It was already happening. This adds fuel.".

Latest Update: Why the Northeast Could Lead a Factory-Built Housing Boom

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.
  • A upcoming economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.
  • Recent findings suggest that berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional new construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Most Americans picture sun-drenched mobile home parks across the South and Southeast when they think of manufactured housing, but more manufactured housing may soon start popping up across the Northeast and West.

A upcoming economic research report from Realtor.com® senior economist Joel Berner takes an in-depth look at the manufactured housing guidelines in the 21st Century Road to Housing Act, which became law in June.

Recent findings suggest that berner found that cities across the Northeast—including Hartford, CT, Allentown, PA, and Albany, NY—have ideal conditions for a manufactured housing boom: “affordable land, unaffordable traditional new construction, and a low share of single-family starter home inventory.”If you’re not quite sure about what “manufactured housing" means, you’re not alone. For years, people seemingly used “mobile home” and “manufactured housing” interchangeably. But they’re not the same thing.

It has been revealed that for one, the “mobile home” classification was retired in 1980, though many still use it colloquially. That year, it was replaced by the term “manufactured home.” Broadly, manufactured homes are those built in a factory and then transported to a site.

For years, federal Housing and Urban Development code required that all manufactured homes have a permanent steel towing frame underneath. New provisions in the Road to Housing Act, meant to spur more affordable housing, eliminated that requirement.

The act further entitles these newly introduced chassis-free homes to the same financing, titling, insurance, taxes, transport, and installation as conventional homes.

The hope is that creating this newly introduced category of manufactured home will help blunt one of the housing industry’s sharpest pain points: affordable starter homes.

Since the COVID-19 pandemic, the number of affordable starter homes for sale has markedly decreased.

It has been revealed that realtor.com research found roughly 300,000 fewer affordable “starter” listings on the market today than before the pandemic. The cost of those starter homes rose from $256,000 in 2019 to $344,000 in 2026. By comparison, the median price of a manufactured home in April 2026 was $134,800.

To understand what metros might see the biggest impact from this upcoming type of manufactured home, Realtor.com scored the 100 largest metro areas on three metrics: the percentage of single-family starter homes (defined as listings priced at or below 80% of the local median) in the area; the relative price-per-square-foot premiums for traditional new construction; and the availability of affordable vacant land.

In a recent development, six of the 10 opportunity metros were in the Northeast, including Hartford; Allentown; Albany; Rochester, NY; Syracuse, NY; and Worcester, MA. Other metros that made the list were Denver; Colorado Springs, CO; Albuquerque, NM; and Spokane, WA.

In Hartford, which ranked first, starter homes account for just 17.9% of single-family inventory, while site-built new construction costs 29.1% more per square foot than existing homes.

In third-ranked Allentown, single-family starter homes made up 22.9% of housing in the area, but upcoming-construction costs were 33.6% more than existing homes. In sixth-ranked Albany, starter homes comprised 31.6% of the single-family inventory, but the price per square foot for new construction is 47% higher than for existing homes.

That’s nothing compared with seventh-ranked Rochester, where 33.7% of homes are starter but site-built new construction costs 97% more per square foot than existing homes.

While the economics in these cities are compelling, another reason manufactured housing may become more popular in these metros is that frigid Northeastern winters limit conventional housing construction. Meanwhile, manufactured housing can be assembled year-round.

Before Hartford, Albany, or any other metro can begin taking advantage of the Road to Housing Act’s new manufactured housing rules, municipal zoning laws will need to change, Berner found.

According to Land Use Labs data cited in the report, only about 17% of zoned land nationwide explicitly permits manufactured housing communities, and many municipalities enforce minimum floor-size rules or design restrictions that block factory-built units.

Breaking: Autistic brains look surprisingly similar on average. Then scientists looked closer.

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (761 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Industry observers note that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism.
  • The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD).
  • The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Industry observers note that brain scans have revealed a surprising pattern in people with autism. Although adults with and without autism highlighted remarkably similar brain activity when researchers compared group averages, a closer examination uncovered striking differences between individuals. These differences were especially pronounced in brain regions involved in understanding and responding to social information.

The findings, published in JNeurosci, suggest that looking at average brain activity may conceal important differences among people with autism spectrum disorder (ASD). The discovery could help scientists better understand why autism varies so widely from person to person and eventually support more personalized approaches to care.

The research was led by Dorit Kliemann and James Traer of the University of Iowa, who worked with collaborators to investigate how brain activity differs between adults with and without autism.

What Brain Scans Reveal When People Watch Movies.

It has been revealed that to explore these differences, the team examined previously collected brain imaging data from Indiana University and Caltech. The recordings captured brain activity as adults with and without autism watched movies from several genres, including animation, action, romantic comedy, and Hitchcockian thrillers.

Recent findings suggest that movies offered researchers a way to study how the brain responds to a constantly changing stream of sights, sounds, and social interactions. Unlike simple laboratory tasks, movies present a rich mixture of information that more closely resembles the complexity of everyday experiences.

Using the imaging data, the researchers trained a computational model to identify connections between brain activity and different elements of the movies. These included visual details, sounds, and more abstract social information, such as interactions between characters.

After training, the model was able to accurately predict activity across several brain systems.

Kliemann explained why this approach is particularly useful for investigating the social challenges sometimes associated with autism: "The computational model allowed us to look for robust brain responses to many different aspects of the complex, dynamic contexts in the movies.".

A Surprising Difference Hidden by Brain Activity Averages.

The most unexpected finding emerged when researchers compared the two groups.

At first, the results suggested relatively little difference. When brain responses were averaged across participants, the model predicted activity in various brain systems similarly for adults with and without autism.

However, the picture changed when the researchers examined how much individual participants differed from others in their own group.

In a recent development, people with autism showed substantially greater variation in their brain responses than participants without autism. In other words, although the overall group averages looked similar, the responses of individual autistic participants were much less alike.

It has been revealed that this increased variability appeared across nearly every brain system examined. The strongest differences occurred in the social brain system, a network of regions involved in processing social information and understanding other people.

Why the Findings Could Change Autism Research.

Recent findings suggest that the results raise notable questions about how scientists investigate autism. Many existing approaches to understanding and treating the condition rely heavily on comparing average measurements from groups of autistic and nonautistic individuals.

But if autistic people show considerable differences in how their brains process information, these averages may obscure some of the most meaningful findings.

Traer described the team's surprise: "We were surprised by the similarity of group averages. The results suggest that we need to focus on understanding the details of individual brain responses. How and why do they differ?".

Rather than searching only for brain activity patterns shared by everyone with autism, the findings point toward the potential value of studying individuals and identifying smaller groups with similar characteristics.

Kliemann highlighted what this could mean for future research and support: "Identifying ASD subgroups may help us build a more precise understanding of the condition and help develop ways to provide individually tailored support.".

The researchers now strategy to investigate how these differences in brain activity relate to variations in autism-related behavior. They hope to determine where and when the differences emerge, how they are connected to individual characteristics, and what might explain them.

Ultimately, the findings suggest that understanding autism may require looking beyond the average brain and paying closer attention to the distinctive ways individuals process the world.
