Scientists discover a hidden hereditary form of aggressive prostate cancer

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1053 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • It has been revealed that scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life.
  • Industry observers note that most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time.
  • In a recent development, among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

It has been revealed that scientists have identified a previously unrecognized inherited form of prostate cancer that, although extremely rare, can lead to aggressive disease relatively early in life. The discovery, made by researchers at the University of British Columbia (UBC), could help doctors identify families with a heightened genetic risk and detect cancer before it spreads.

Industry observers note that most cancers develop as genetic changes build up in cells over time. However, approximately 5% to 10% are associated with inherited mutations that can be passed from parents to their children, creating a cancer risk that may extend across generations.

In a recent development, among the most familiar examples are mutations in the BRCA1 and BRCA2 genes. These inherited changes can substantially raise the likelihood of breast, ovarian, pancreatic, and prostate cancers. Testing for BRCA mutations has reshaped cancer prevention and treatment by allowing people with elevated risks to receive earlier screening and preventive care.

Sources indicate that now, a study published in Cancer Discovery points to another gene, CDK12, as a potentially vital marker of inherited prostate cancer risk. After examining genetic information from more than 4,500 people with aggressive prostate cancer, the researchers discovered five unrelated men with inherited mutations in CDK12. Every one of these men developed metastatic prostate cancer between ages 44 and 62, meaning the cancer had spread beyond the prostate.

"What's striking is that every patient we identified with this inherited mutation had already developed metastatic disease by the time they were diagnosed," said senior author Dr. Alexander Wyatt, associate professor of urologic sciences in the UBC faculty of medicine and UBC President's Excellence Chair in Precision Oncology. "The opportunity now is to identify these families earlier and give people the chance to benefit from enhanced screening, when there are still curative treatment options.".

A Hidden Genetic Cause of Aggressive Prostate Cancer.

The discovery challenges a longstanding assumption about CDK12. Scientists previously believed that harmful changes in this gene developed spontaneously inside cancer cells rather than being inherited from a parent.

It has been revealed that to investigate whether the inherited mutations were actually contributing to the disease, the team examined the patients' tumors for a distinctive pattern of genetic damage associated with loss of CDK12 function. This molecular fingerprint helped connect the inherited mutations to the development of their cancers.

It has been revealed that "The tumors provided us with a genetic signature that pointed directly back to CDK12," remarked lead author Dr. Sofie Tolmeijer, a postdoctoral fellow in the Wyatt lab. "It gave us compelling evidence that these inherited mutations were playing a direct role in causing their cancer.".

The findings emerged from a broad international research effort involving UBC, BC Cancer, the Vancouver Coastal Health Research Institute, and the University of Washington, along with scientists at institutions in Australia, the Netherlands, Spain, and Belgium.

Despite the potentially serious consequences, inherited CDK12 mutations appear to be exceptionally uncommon. The researchers found them in approximately one out of every 1,000 people with aggressive prostate cancer. Even at that low frequency, they estimate that hundreds of families around the world could be affected.

Sources indicate that "While this mutation is extremely rare, the discovery could be lifesaving for the families who carry it," said Dr. Tolmeijer. "Finding one person with an inherited mutation gives us the opportunity to identify other family members at risk and help them take action before cancer develops or spreads.".

Genetic Testing Could Help Detect Prostate Cancer Earlier.

One of the most promising implications of the discovery is that doctors may not need to develop entirely latest testing technology to put the findings into practice.

The researchers recommend including CDK12 in standard genetic testing panels used to assess hereditary prostate cancer risk. These panels examine multiple genes associated with inherited cancer susceptibility, helping identify individuals who may benefit from closer medical monitoring.

Importantly, the clinical technology required to detect CDK12 mutations already exists. That could make expanding genetic testing relatively straightforward, potentially reducing the time and expense needed to bring the discovery into routine patient care.

It has been revealed that "One of the most exciting aspects of this discovery is that we already have the technology needed to act on it," mentioned Dr. Wyatt, who is also a senior research scientist at the Vancouver Prostate Centre and senior scientist at BC Cancer. "Adding CDK12 to existing genetic tests is relatively straightforward, which means this discovery could move from the research lab into clinical care much more quickly.".

Could the Same Mutation Increase Ovarian Cancer Risk?

The study also uncovered clues suggesting that inherited CDK12 mutations might be associated with ovarian cancer, although more research is needed to establish whether they increase the risk.

In a recent development, several of the men with inherited CDK12 mutations had relatives with a history of ovarian cancer. The investigators also identified another person who had ovarian cancer and carried an inherited CDK12 mutation. Analysis of that person's tumor revealed the same characteristic genetic signature seen in the prostate cancer cases.

Together, these observations suggest that CDK12 could potentially play a role in hereditary cancer risk beyond the prostate. Further studies will be needed to determine how strongly the mutations are associated with ovarian cancer and whether they should influence screening recommendations.

Sources indicate that for families carrying these rare mutations, the potential benefits of identifying their genetic risk could be substantial. Earlier testing may give relatives the opportunity to receive closer surveillance and, if cancer develops, begin treatment before it reaches an advanced stage.

"With the right genetic testing and screening programs, we envision a future where no one who inherits one of these mutations dies from cancer," noted Dr. Wyatt.

In a recent development, the research received funding from the Prostate Cancer Foundation, Terry Fox Research Institute, Canadian Cancer Society, Canadian Institutes of Health Research, Michael Smith Health Research BC, U.S. National Institutes of Health, BC Cancer Foundation, and other funding partners.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.
  • Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:48 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Updated with Wednesday stock prices:.

Recent findings suggest that dell Technologies Inc. and HP Inc. delivered strong earnings and revenue beats as they posted their latest financial results today.

However, the companies have very different prospects going forward as they try to come to terms with the diverging fortunes of the artificial intelligence server and personal computer markets they serve.

Dell reported third-quarter adjusted earnings of $9.45 per share on revenue of $54.94 billion, a stunning result that blew past Wall Street’s expectations of just $6.59 per share in earnings and $49.32 billion in sales.

According to recent reports, the company’s revenue more than doubled from a year earlier thanks to the sky-high demand for the AI servers and related data center infrastructure equipment it sells. Dell’s Infrastructure Solutions Group delivered sales of $41.97 billion during the quarter, far in excess of the Street’s target of $35.27 billion. Of that, around $22 billion came from direct AI-optimized server sales, the company said. That segment was up 291% annually.

“We are now a different company, with the Infrastructure Solutions Group driving the vast majority of our profit and growth,” mentioned Dell Vice Chairman and Chief Operating Officer Jeff Clarke (pictured). He added that Dell now has more than 7,500 customers buying its AI servers.

It has been revealed that the Street liked what it saw, with Dell’s stock rising more than 3% after hours, putting the brakes on an 11% decline earlier, during the regular trading session. Patch: However, on another down day for tech stocks Wednesday, Dell’s shares were falling almost 8% before the market cut some of those losses and Dell was falling only a fraction of a point.

Dell’s performance in the quarter sets a new precedent for infrastructure systems companies, stated longtime technology industry analyst Dave Vellante, chief analyst at theCUBE Research, SiliconANGLE Media’s sister market research firm.

“Dell has transformed from a PC tech giant into a dominant enterprise infrastructure provider and industry bellwether,” he said. “What’s most astounding to me is that I’ve always considered AWS to be Dell’s most formidable competitor. Dell is now significantly larger than AWS on a trailing 12-month revenue basis and is growing at a rate that’s more than double that of AWS, Azure and on a par with Google Cloud.”.

Dell is raising its forecast for AI servers in the coming fiscal years, and now sees sales rising to a staggering $78 billion, ahead of the Street’s target of $74 billion. At present, the tech giant has an even bigger order backlog of $132.3 billion for AI servers. “Every order is verified for access to capital, end customer quality, trade and export compliance and access to land and power,” Clarke told analysts in response to a question about the reliability of that backlog.

Vellante said Dell’s operating leverage is just as impressive, with its operating income, net profit and earnings per share all growing at rates over two-times its revenue growth.

“Its massive backlog and strong product execution allow it to be selective,” the analyst mentioned. “Thus the quality of its revenue and its backlog is very high, and the tech giant is well-positioned for the next several quarters. Current market signals point to a structural change in tech where vendors that are in a position to help customers transform and drive fresh levels of productivity are poised to win over the long term. We increasingly see Dell as one of those leaders.”.

Besides servers, Dell still has a big business in the PC market. Its Client Services Group was once the company’s biggest segment, but its revenue is now dwarfed by AI server sales. During the quarter, it generated revenue of $12.89 billion, below the Street’s forecast of $14.33 billion.

The reason for that miss is that the global PC market is currently enduring a sharp decline. Last month, Gartner Inc. reported a stunning 22% drop in global PC shipments in the third quarter, citing the increased costs of components such as memory chips, which have led to higher prices and compelled many people to hold onto their older laptops for longer.

The miserable state of PC sales makes HP’s latest quarterly results seem even more impressive than they were. However, the company’s cautious outlook suggests that its incoming Chief Executive Emma Walmsley (pictured, right) will have her work cut out when she assumes the role full time on Jan. 4, when she’s slated to take over from interim CEO Bruce Broussard.

Sources indicate that HP reported fourth-quarter adjusted earnings of 83 cents per share, surpassing the analyst consensus estimate that called for a profit of just 75 cents per share. Revenue for the period came to $16 billion, up 9% and above the Street’s target of $15.4 billion.

In a recent development, HP’s stock briefly surged more than 17% after-hours, before promptly surrendering all of those gains in under an hour. It was down just under a percentage point at the time of writing. Update: On Wednesday, investors appeared to change their minds again, as the stock was rising more than 12%.

In a recent development, investors had low expectations of HP given the shoddy state of the PC market. The company has been trying to mitigate the situation somewhat by raising its prices, but it couldn’t stop its profit margins from declining in the quarter.

The market was eagerly anticipating HP’s guidance to try and get a lid on whether or not the PC market has any prospect of recovery in the near future, but the company disappointed by refusing to provide any. All it would say is that it forecasts free cash flow in the current quarter to be $3 billion, plus or minus $100 million. Analysts are targeting free cash flow of $3.3 billion.

Sources indicate that HP hasn’t been helped by the fact that it has been without a CEO since PayPal Holdings Inc. surprisingly swooped in to poach its former leader Enrique Lores in February. Broussard has held the fort for close to nine months now, but the firm did at least finally name a successor in Walmsley, who will begin her tenure next year. She formerly led the pharmaceutical giant GSK Plc.

Walmsley has a tough act to follow, however, for Broussard has done rather well in his efforts to cope with the PC market downturn and the higher component costs. Although the stock was up and down today, it’s still up 25% in the year to date.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Centralized platform for submitting, managing out-of-network billing disputes launches" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The Trump administration has launched a new online portal for payers, providers and other stakeholders to manage and monitor disputes under the federal Independent Dispute Resolution process.

Recent findings suggest that the IDR Gateway went online Nov. 13 and was officially unveiled Nov. 20. It replaces the web forms parties previously used to manage disputes, most of which will no longer be available outside of the centralized platform after Jan. 15, 2027, per a government fact sheet.

Payers will eventually be required to register on IDR Gateway so that it is easier for providers to identify the correct party, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services stated earlier this year when finalizing an overhaul of No Surprises Act protocols. That registration feature will be added “in the future on a rolling basis,” CMS said last week, with others like in-portal negotiation similarly rolling out over time “to improve accountability and reduce unnecessary filings,” the agency said last spring.

For now, the IDR Gateway allows parties and their representatives to initiate a dispute, respond to proposed selections of IDR entities and submit a payment offer. Its other tools allow users to view, search, set up notifications and broadly analyze open disputes for their organization; an IDR Gateway Dashboard, CMS mentioned, offers a color-coded donut chart breaking down an organization’s different types of open disputes by phase, while another tool can generate detailed reports of dispute line items.

It has been revealed that the administration also touted security measures inherent to the new portal. These include a new sign-up process that requires users to verify their identity with an approved credential service provider, and other protocols like a terms and conditions agreement that notes that unauthorized users could be subject to criminal prosecution.

The baseball-style IDR process enacted under the No Surprises Act, intended to handle out-of-network billing disputes away from the patient’s purview, has become a point of contention amid dispute volumes and payouts well beyond legislators’ expectations.

Arbitrators’ decisions have largely favored providers over payers (85% of decisions went toward providers last year), which alongside court decisions that tweaked CMS’ processes further toward provider preferences, has triggered outright condemnation from payers who have turned to lawsuits, restrictive policies and lobbying in a bit to reform the process. Recent analyses have pegged the IDR process’ impact for employer intends at $8.4 billion in 2025 and total costs associated with the process at $22 billion for that same year.

Lawmakers including the No Surprises Act’s chief authors have stated they hope to pass latest legislation to fix or fully replace the IDR process, with December’s must-pass budget bill now looking like a likely vehicle for such a change.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising.
  • It has been revealed that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

The digital world has revolutionized how real estate is marketed and sold, placing a premium on strategic online presence and data-driven advertising. Among the myriad online tools available, Schema Markup stands out as an extremely potent weapon for real estate agents. This article offers a comprehensive look at how real estate agents can effectively use Schema Markup to bolster their online presence, increase organic reach, and drive sales.

It has been revealed that before discussing its application, let's first demystify what Schema Markup is. Schema Markup, also known as Structured Data, is a form of microdata. Once added to a webpage, it creates an enhanced description (commonly known as a rich snippet), which appears in search results. Developed by a collaborative team from Google, Yahoo!, Bing, and Yandex, Schema.org was rolled out in 2011 to create and support a common set of schemas for structured data markup on web pages.

To break it down simply, Schema Markup tells the search engine what your data means, not just what it indicates. This enhanced understanding allows search engines to present more detailed and accurate snippets of your site to people, increasing click-through rates (CTR), boosting organic search rankings, and potentially improving conversion rates.

Why Real Estate Agents Need Schema Markup.

Recent findings suggest that schema Markup is incredibly beneficial to real estate professionals. The real estate industry is hyper-local, and search engine queries reflect this. Buyers and sellers are often searching with a specific location in mind. A real estate agent using Schema Markup can provide rich, location-based information directly in search results, making their listings more likely to be clicked on. It's an opportunity to outshine competitors and improve visibility in local search results.

Furthermore, Schema Markup helps real estate websites become more comprehensible to search engines. This enhanced understanding translates into more accurate categorization, increased visibility, and a better chance of appearing in relevant search results. In a landscape where digital prominence equates to business success, Schema Markup is no longer a luxury but a necessity for every real estate agent.

#156672. A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

📅 18 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 6m • 📚 Deep Dive (1138 w)

A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

📅 18 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1138 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that for decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder.
  • The condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening.
  • Industry observers note that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that for decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a fresh treatment.

The condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A new study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.

Industry observers note that the researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.

In a recent development, "This study has revealed a latest target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," states Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before.".

Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation.

Sources indicate that MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.

For roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.

To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.

Their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an key role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.

Recent findings suggest that the consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.

According to recent reports, "We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients.".

Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research.

The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.

Dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, notes the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.

Sources indicate that "This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she says.

To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.

Using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments revealed that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.

These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.

Existing Drug Indicates Promise for a Upcoming Treatment.

The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.

Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.

According to recent reports, baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.

Doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.

Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.

The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.

Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases.

The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.

It has been revealed that researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.

If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.

"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," notes Professor Rogers.

Sources indicate that professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes
Academic hospital heads petition Congress for 2-year delay to CMS' 340B cuts" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

Dozens of academic health system and teaching hospital chief executives are turning to Congress in a bid to blunt a controversial subsidy cut coming to Medicare Part B in the latest year.

Earlier this month, the Centers for Medicare and Medicaid Services locked in prepares to reduce reimbursements for outpatient drugs dispensed by participants in the 340B Drug Pricing Program during the 2027 calendar year.

Specifically, the agency said it will move from the current rate of average sales price (ASP) plus 6% down to ASP minus 28%, with a corresponding 7.5% increase in non-drug outpatient payments to maintain budget neutrality. CMS said the change will reduce Original Medicare drug payments by an estimated $4.35 billion and drug payments from beneficiaries by $1.1 billion during the policy’s first year.

Hospital groups—particularly those that chiefly represent nonprofit or safety-net hospitals—have denounced the proposal’s disproportionate effect on hospitals participating in the decades-old subsidy program, as well as a gift to for-profit hospitals that do not participate but will benefit from the budget-neutral offset.

With their formal opposition to the policy’s proposal set aside by CMS, 95 executives whose organizations are members of the Association of American Medical Colleges have now penned a letter to leaders of the House and the Senate pleading for a two-year delay to the rate cut’s implementation.

“This policy will exacerbate already negative Medicare margins at a time when teaching hospitals are already grappling with rising financial challenges resulting from inflation, workforce shortages, manufacturer-driven restrictions on the 340B program and an expected rise in uncompensated care costs,” they wrote.

It has been revealed that the executives acknowledged that the final policy’s rate of ASP minus 28% is “slightly smaller” than CMS’ initial proposal of ASP minus 33.4%, but said the change was still a threat to the country’s healthcare safety net. They noted the cuts represent a nearly $5.5 billion reduction that would be disproportionately shouldered by AAMC-member teaching hospitals—who comprise 17% of all impacted hospitals—but will see almost $3 billion of that total.

According to recent reports, those funds are necessary to finance critical care services at academic hospitals including trauma care, inpatient behavioral care, transplant surgery and labor and delivery, the signatories warned lawmakers. They also noted that their institutions are major referral hubs that accept “the most complex transfer cases from lower acuity settings, such as rural and community hospitals,” in a way that for-profit hospitals and others who will benefit from the final rule do not.

“While we understand that Congress has an interest in improving the 340B program, and are broadly supportive of meaningful transparency and accountability for covered entities, we also strongly believe that cutting Medicare payment to 340B hospitals is not the appropriate policy mechanism to achieve these goals,” they wrote. “Therefore, we respectfully request that you support a two-year delay in the [Outpatient Prospective Payment System] rule’s payment cuts for 340B-acquired drugs.”.

Among the letter’s 95 signatories were the heads of Cedars-Sinai, Stanford Health Care, Yale Latest Haven Health, Tampa General Hospital, Rush University System for Health, Mass General Brigham, Nebraska Medicine, RWJBarnabas Health, NewYork-Presbyterian, UNC Health and School of Medicine, OHSU, Jefferson Health, Penn Medicine, Vanderbilt Health and Froedtert ThedaCare.

Sources indicate that the academic health systems and hospitals’ turn to lawmakers comes after their rebukes of CMS’ 340B policy have fallen on deaf ears. The agency and broader Trump administration have often sided with critics of the subsidy program on related initiatives like a pilot rebate program, citing 340B’s rapid growth and contribution to increased healthcare spending. A Health and Human Services Office of the Assistant Secretary for Planning and Evaluation policy brief defending the rate cut made those views crystal clear with claims that the program has incentivized provider consolidation while doing little to serve patients’ needs.

Meanwhile, Congress, spurred by public pressure to reduce healthcare costs, has proposed its own legislative fixes to 340B. Though each bill aims to preserve the program and subsidize safety-net care, some are more friendly to the hospital industry than others.

#156669. A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

📅 20 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 4m • 📚 Deep Dive (894 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Sciencedaily ↗ Open Full Page

A study of 30,000 people reveals which antidepressants may work best

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (894 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • A newly introduced review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.
  • The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac).
  • But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A newly introduced review has found some antidepressants may be more effective than others at helping people reduce the severity of their symptoms of depression over the long term.

The research, published in The Lancet Psychiatry, found people taking escitalopram (commonly sold as Lexapro), duloxetine (Cymbalta) and agomelatine (Valdoxan) were more likely to report improved symptoms over the long term than those taking fluoxetine (Prozac). For those taking Lexapro and Cymbalta, they were also more likely to stay on their medications.

But does that mean these are the best antidepressants?

Around one in seven Australians will experience depression during their lifetime.

In a recent development, treatment can involve psychological therapies, social support and lifestyle changes, such as doing more exercise. For some people, these approaches may be enough to support recovery. For others, adding an antidepressant can be an key part of treatment.

In 2024-2025, 3.8 million Australians were dispensed a prescription for an antidepressant.

For adults with depression, clinical guidelines recommend continuing antidepressants for at least six months, and preferably 12 months, after an acceptable response to treatment is achieved.

In a recent development, if, after six to 12 months, the depressive episode has resolved, it may be appropriate to reduce, and eventually stop the antidepressant. But symptoms can occur when discontinuing antidepressants so it’s important this is done gradually, in consultation with a doctor.

Recent findings suggest that studies of real world antidepressant prescribing patterns in Australia suggest many people take antidepressants for longer than this. One 2022 study found nearly a quarter of those prescribed antidepressants were still receiving prescriptions for them two years later.

Another Australian study found people take antidepressants for an average of four years.

The fresh review set out to compare how well different antidepressants help people maintain improvements in depression. The researchers also compared how acceptable the medicines were to the people taking them. They measured this by looking at the proportion of people who stopped treatment for any reason during the study period.

The researchers identified and reviewed 115 randomized controlled trials, involving more than 30,000 people. The researchers classified long-term use as six months or more. Their main analysis combined the results of 35 trials that directly compared one antidepressant with another.

They found that three antidepressants – escitalopram, duloxetine and agomelatine – were associated with a greater likelihood of sustained response than fluoxetine.

People taking escitalopram or duloxetine were also less likely to drop out of the trials than those taking fluoxetine.

The findings are interesting as escitalopram (Lexapro) is the most commonly prescribed antidepressant in Australia. It ranked number 13 out of all PBS-dispensed prescriptions in 2024–25. Duloxetine was number 45, but agomelatine isn’t available on the PBS.

Recent findings suggest that the findings suggest some antidepressants may be more effective than others at sustaining a response to treatment, but the results are far from definitive. More than half of the studies included in the main analysis were assessed as having a high risk of bias.

This means some of the differences between antidepressants may reflect limitations in the original studies rather than genuine differences between the medicines. Some medicines were also supported by very few studies, making comparisons less certain.

Sources indicate that another aspect to keep in mind when considering these results is what is meant by “long term.” The trials directly comparing antidepressants typically followed participants for around six months after they first started taking the medication. Only six followed people for longer than six months.

This means we still know relatively little about how the effectiveness of different antidepressants compares over longer periods. This is notable given the average time people take them is much longer.

In a recent development, importantly, these findings reflect average outcomes across groups of people. They can’t tell us which antidepressant will work best for any particular person.

People respond differently to antidepressants, and what makes a medicine acceptable to one person may not be acceptable to another. While the researchers used trial drop-out rates as a measure of acceptability, this doesn’t necessarily capture people’s experiences of taking these medicines.

Sources indicate that for someone taking an antidepressant, acceptability might not be so binary. It may involve a trade-off between how the medication improves symptoms, its side effects, and how the medicine affects their everyday life.

Industry observers note that continuing to take an antidepressant doesn’t necessarily mean someone finds it acceptable. Some people experience withdrawal symptoms when trying to stop, which can make discontinuation difficult.

Recent findings suggest that ultimately, determining if an antidepressant is right for you, and which is the best fit, depends on many factors. These include your symptoms, other health conditions, previous experiences with medicines, potential side effects and what matters most to you.

If you’re taking an antidepressant that’s working well for you, the findings of this study aren’t a reason to switch.

And if you’re considering starting, changing or stopping an antidepressant, discuss your options with your doctor.

When John F. Kennedy came home to Hyannis Port for his first Thanksgiving as president, his father still had the best seat in the house.

Industry observers note that joseph P. Kennedy presided over the family table, the children ate first, and the cranberries served with dinner came from bogs near the family’s Cape Cod retreat.

Industry observers note that five years earlier, it was what happened after Thanksgiving dinner that the family would remember. John, then a Massachusetts senator, slipped into the study off the living room with his father.

According to recent reports, he had a list of reasons to think twice about running for president. Joseph had an answer for every one.

By the time they emerged, the Kennedys had a campaign to proposal.

The house where that conversation took place began as a summer rental. In 1926, Joseph and his wife, Rose, brought their children to Malcolm Cottage, a waterfront home overlooking Nantucket Sound. John was just 9.

It has been revealed that according to the John F. Kennedy Hyannis Museum, Joseph bought the property two years later for $25,000 and expanded the house to accommodate his growing family.

It has been revealed that john eventually bought a place of his own behind his parents’ home. His brother Robert and sister-in-law Ethel came to own an adjoining property.

Together, the three residences formed the 6-acre compound, an arrangement that put several generations of Kennedys within walking distance of Thanksgiving dinner at the Significant House.

Recent findings suggest that in "White House by the Sea," author Kate Storey describes a family with surprisingly little use for a formal seating proposal. Joseph and Rose took opposite ends of the mahogany table.

Everyone else picked a spot. Family cook Ziptha Anderson remembered far less flexibility when it came to carving the bird.

“They all like the same thing—the white meat,” she noted.

The weather had a say in the menu, too. A chilly Thanksgiving called for clam broth, while a mild afternoon meant tomato juice to start.

Industry observers note that dinner was at 1 p.m. in Storey’s account of the 1956 gathering, which still left the family time for Mass and a sail before they made their way to the table.

By Thanksgiving 1961, the guest list included 13 Kennedy adults and 15 Kennedy children. There was room for another family, too. Paul Fay, then undersecretary of the Navy, joined the celebration with his wife and their three children.

One family outing took the president and several of his siblings to the skating rink in Hyannis named for their late brother, Joseph Jr. John watched while Ted and his sisters rented skates and played tag on the ice.

Back at the compound, Bobby and Ted also got a touch football game going. That evening, the adults sat down to Vermont turkey, candied sweet potatoes, and their choice of pies.

It has been revealed that ted found another way to work up an appetite in 1979. A United Press International photographer caught the senator waving from his boat as he took relatives and friends sailing off Hyannis Port before Thanksgiving dinner.

In a recent development, ethel carried on hosting Thanksgiving at Hyannis Port long after her children had families of their own. In 2010, she enlisted her son Robert to bring home two live turkeys so her grandchildren could see the birds up close. One promptly escaped.

“For three days they chased it everywhere,” Ethel told the Cape Cod Times.

It has been revealed that A couple of months later, the newspaper ran a story about a turkey causing trouble in nearby Centerville, where it had even taken on a moving postal truck. Ethel called the newsroom. She thought she knew where the bird had come from.

Half of voters said they are paying more this year in premiums and out-of-pocket costs, according to a new national poll.

Lake Research Partners and Bellwether Research & Consulting surveyed 1,000 voters between Oct. 20 and Oct. 28 on behalf of the National Health Council, and 50% stated their premiums and out-of-pocket costs are higher this year compared to last year. Among those with commercial insurance, 63% said their premiums have risen, and 60% said their out-of-pocket costs have grown year-over-year.

Sources indicate that in addition, 25% of those surveyed mentioned they had a claim for a prescription denied, and 24% said they waited more than two weeks for a prior authorization decision. Twenty-one percent said that they struggled to find a specialist.

Healthcare costs and the broader economy were major factors in Democrats' significant victories in the latest midterm election. And the NHC poll finds that voters expect Congress to act on addressing the costs that they face.

Most of the surveyed voters (78%) said they believe that the healthcare system warrants major changes or a complete overhaul, and 84% said they would support a candidate that would make it a priority to reform the healthcare insurance system.

However, 74% of those surveyed rated the effort from elected officials to address affordability and access as either fair or poor.

Recent findings suggest that “Holding onto a initiative isn’t the same as being protected by it. Patients are watching their costs rise and their coverage change, and they’re worried about what that means for their families down the road,” said Randall Rutta, CEO of the National Health Council, in an announcement. “The new Congress has a real opportunity to change that, and patients across the country will be watching.”.

The survey highlights a number of potential policies that would have broad voter support. For example, 91% of those surveyed mentioned they would support eliminating surprise medical bills and policies to require price transparency.

It has been revealed that in addition, 90% noted they would back efforts to reduce out-of-pocket costs, while 89% said they favor requiring health looks to cover treatments that were prescribed by doctors. Eighty-eight percent support efforts to increase screening and early detection for medical risks.

Recent findings suggest that "Voters aren't asking lawmakers to talk about health care differently," stated Christine Matthews, president of Bellwether Research and Consulting, in the release. "They want to see it work differently. Reform is a priority they expect the upcoming Congress to deliver on.".

Why don't weight-loss drugs like Ozempic and Wegovy work for everyone?

📅 19 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (791 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.
  • Sources indicate that research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions.
  • These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Medications like Ozempic and Wegovy, which contain semaglutide — a GLP‑1 receptor agonist that helps regulate blood sugar, appetite and body weight — have become household names and important pillars in obesity management for the medical profession.

Sources indicate that research has shown GLP-1 medications reduce body weight by an average of 15 percent when used weekly for 68 weeks and combined with lifestyle interventions. This is because semaglutide acts on the brain to increase the feeling of fullness and to decrease appetite.

These medications don’t work the same way for everyone, however. Our multidisciplinary research team at the University of Alberta is working to improve obesity care for people of all ages and to understand why some people respond better to semaglutide than others, and how their weight loss can be maintained over time.

We are investigating the role of energy metabolism as a potentially key piece in a complex puzzle.

Research has shown semaglutide medications to improve quality of life, blood markers such as sugar or cholesterol, strength and overall health. Weight loss is only one measure of how well they work.

We are exploring whether people’s responses to these medications could lie in individual factors such as genetics, metabolism, body composition, lifestyle, microbiota, associated diseases, age and sex.

Energy metabolism may also be an vital piece of this puzzle. This is a measure of the total calories consumed (in) and the total calories burned (out). We burn calories all the time: for vital processes like breathing and thinking, physical activities like going to the gym and the everyday act of digesting food.

It has been revealed that when we lose weight, our bodies naturally need less energy. But sometimes, the body goes into an extra “energy-saving mode,” burning even fewer calories than we would expect. This is called metabolic adaptation, or adaptive thermogenesis.

Think of it like a light bulb that automatically dims to save electricity. This is one reason why losing weight can become more difficult over time, sometimes leading to a weight-loss plateau.

Changes in body weight and composition (the amount of fat and fat-free mass in our bodies) play an vital role in energy metabolism. Both fat and fat-free mass use energy, even when we are resting. As we lose these tissues, our bodies naturally burn fewer calories.

It has been revealed that researchers are still trying to understand whether weight-loss medications influence these processes differently. If we can understand how our bodies use energy during and after weight loss, this could help us develop better strategies for maintaining weight loss over the long term.

In a recent development, we published a recent review of studies investigating the effects of GLP-1 therapies on energy utilization. We found a few studies exploring how semaglutide affects resting energy use, with findings that were neutral or inconclusive.

The question of how semaglutide impacts energy use is an emerging area of study, and remains an open question for exploration.

It has been revealed that at the University of Alberta, we have a gold-standard method to measure energy utilization called a whole-room indirect calorimeter. This is a rare research facility and is similar to a hotel suite that can precisely measure each component of energy use. This room can isolate the effects of changes in someone’s calorie burning at rest, after eating and during exercise.

Sources indicate that we are at the moment recruiting research participants with blood sugar regulation concerns, such as insulin resistance or diabetes, who are about to start semaglutide treatment. We will follow their weight loss journey over six months to investigate changes in body weight and composition, and energy utilization using sophisticated approaches.

Understanding how semaglutide influences energy use and body composition, and how these changes interact, could be an notable step toward explaining why individuals respond differently to weight-loss treatment.

This will allow us to contribute to more personalized approaches to obesity and Type 2 diabetes management in the future. Having a better understanding of how energy use changes with semaglutide-induced weight loss will also help us to better anticipate potential non-responders (people who do not lose weight) and offer alternative treatments sooner in their health journey.

Importantly, current evidence suggests that if you are taking semaglutide or considering starting treatment, you should make a few lifestyle changes.

In a recent development, materials provided by The Conversation. Original written by Giovanna Guimaraes Lopes Bergamasco, Andrea M. Haqq, Carla Prado, and Rachel J. Skow. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

UPDATED 18:49 EST / NOVEMBER 24 2026.

Artificial intelligence infrastructure startup Marlowe AI Inc. has closed a huge $227 million seed round led by Accel.

Bessemer, Altimeter, Emergence Capital and a number of other institutional bakers chipped in as well. They were joined by a large group of angel investors that included the chief executives of Palo Alto Networks Inc, Uber Technologies Inc., Box Inc. and Dropbox Inc. GeekWire reported on Monday that Marlowe is valued at $1.15 billion.

Marlowe was founded last year by CEO Dan Lewis and Chief Technology Officer Kutta Srinivasan. Lewis previously headed the Microsoft Corp. unit responsible for Copilot Studio, the tech giant’s AI agent development tool. Srinivasan was the techical lead of the manufacturer’s AI infrastructure group.

Industry observers note that marlowe is building AI data centers for inference workloads. The company will optimize each facility for a specific inference workload category by tailoring its chip mix, network configuration and software. Marlowe believes that its approach will provide better hardware efficiency than general-purpose graphics card clusters.

“Even modest gains in network architecture, power oversubscription, AI-driven fleet operations, and workload-specific inference optimization multiply to create a durable, 2-3x overall advantage in performance, availability, resiliency, and cost,” Lewis and Srinivasan wrote in Marlowe’s launch blog post.

The organization aims to bring its first data center online  next month. It’s based on hardware from Etched Inc., an inference chip startup that was valued at $21 billion in August.

Recent findings suggest that graphics cards often use only a small fraction of their maximum clock speed to avoid overheating. Etched’s chip is less prone to overheating and can therefore operate at higher clock speeds, which boosts model performance. The company notes that its accelerator provides “multiple times the FLOPs density” of graphics cards.

It has been revealed that etched ships its chips as part of custom-made inference racks. According to the company, the systems feature an interconnect that can perform some data movement tasks more than four times faster than competing silicon. Etched’s rack design also includes custom power management and cooling components.

Marlowe’s second facility will come online in the second quarter of 2027. It will host racks based on Advanced Micro Devices Inc.’s Helios design. A Helios rack hosts 72 AMD graphics cards along with central processing units and Pensando data processing units, or DPUs. The DPUs offload networking tasks from the other chips to leave more computing capacity for AI models.

Helios racks’ networking and power delivery links are arranged in a configuration that reduces the need for manual cable maintenance. Additionally, the coolant lines feature a so-called quick-disconnect design. They can be plugged and unplugged without the specialized tools usually needed for the task.

According to recent reports, geekWire reported that Marlowe has also signed a letter of intent for a third data center. According to the publication, each of the company’s planned facilities will provide tens of megawatts of computing capacity. One megawatt is enough to power several hundred homes.

Marlowe will use the proceeds from its seed round to finance hardware purchases and hire engineers.

Fewer choices available to enrollees on ACA exchanges: RWJF" style="max-width:100%; height:auto; border-radius:8px;" loading="lazy">

The number of regions where patients have limited choices for Affordable Care Act prepares is on the rise, according to a new analysis.

The Robert Wood Johnson Foundation report found that for the 2027 blueprint year, there are more than 200 counties in which there is only one insurer available, and close to 1,000 where there are just two plans available for consumers to choose from.

This makes for an increase of 50% from the 2026 plan year, with more than a third of counties having limited options on the ACA's marketplaces for 2027.

Most states (39) will have at least one county where plan choices are limited for enrollees. For about half of these states, this is the norm and aligns with 2026, but for the rest, this marks a significant shift, the RWJF researchers wrote in the report.

Recent findings suggest that "For the individual market as a whole, the decline in participation is sobering but not a fatal blow," per the report. "The presence of federal and some state subsidies provides an vital backstop that will likely prevent a complete meltdown.".

"Yet the prospect of a growing number of counties with little insurer participation is grim, and likely will not bode well for premium increases, morbidity or enrollment going forward," according to the report.

Recent findings suggest that the foundation cites a recent analysis from Wakely that found the individual market declined by 16% in the first six months of 2026. The end of the enhanced premium tax credits, cost pressures and growing administrative burdens are likely to contribute to worsening trends in this space.

According to recent reports, for instance, ACA marketplace exits from Cigna, CareSource and Medica are having a significant impact in Iowa and Indiana for the coming initiative year, the researchers found. In the latter case, most Indiana counties have two or fewer plan choices.

In a recent development, however, there are some bright spots, RWJF researchers wrote. There are certain insurers participating in the exchanges who have beefed up their footprints, and there is a smattering of upcoming entrants. Oscar Health, for example, is planning the largest growth, entering a new state and adding new counties in some of the states it already serves.

Some insurers, like Centene and UnitedHealthcare, are making strategic exits in some markets while entering others, for a neutral impact on their footprints overall.

Insurers like Antidote Health and Peak Health are also entering fresh regions—even if on a limited basis in some cases—which can help staunch the bleeding.

It has been revealed that blue Cross Blue Shield prepares also often play a key role in limited markets, as in close to 80% of counties with a single insurer, that payer is a Blues plan. In addition, in 12% of counties, the single insurer is Elevance Health, which operates plans as Anthem Blue Cross Blue Shield.

Industry observers note that "This suggests that were it not for the somewhat unique role of Blues looks as a backstop, the threat of a bare county might be higher," per the report. "Single-state Blues, in particular, are under social and political pressure to participate in much if not all of their state, and do not feel as free to exit unprofitable counties as are publicly traded insurers.".

#156659. Industry News: Powerful upcoming weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

Industry News: Powerful upcoming weight-loss drug helps patients cut knee pain in half

📅 20 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1124 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Sciencedaily

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle.
  • The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total.
  • It has been revealed that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

For people living with painful knee osteoarthritis (OA), even simple activities like walking, climbing stairs, or getting out of a chair can become a struggle. Excess body weight can make these challenges even worse. Now, two major clinical trials suggest that a powerful experimental weight-loss drug could provide substantial relief.

The two phase 3 trials, led by Northwestern University, included more than 1,000 participants in total. People receiving the highest dose of retatrutide, an experimental injectable weight-loss medication, lost an average of about 25% of their body weight. When researchers combined the findings from both trials, they found that approximately two-thirds of participants treated with retatrutide reported a reduction in knee pain of at least 50%. By comparison, only 38% of those given a placebo experienced that level of relief.

It has been revealed that the benefits extended beyond weight loss and improved knee pain. Participants also indicated reductions in blood pressure, blood lipid levels, and inflammation throughout the body.

Recent findings suggest that findings from both studies were published on Nov. 8 in the New England Journal of Medicine.

"The findings are really saying for people who are overweight and have OA, if you lose a significant amount of weight with this treatment, there is a good chance that you're going to get a meaningful reduction in your knee pain," noted corresponding author Dr. Thomas Schnitzer, professor of physical medicine and rehabilitation, anesthesiology and medicine (rheumatology) at Northwestern University Feinberg School of Medicine.

"A major factor is that you're loading your knees less and therefore, there's less pain and it allows you to increase your function.".

Industry observers note that philip Conaghan, a study co-author and professor of musculoskeletal medicine at the University of Leeds in the United Kingdom, presented results from one of the trials, TRIUMPH-4, on Nov. 8 at the American College of Rheumatology annual meeting in Orlando, Florida. Findings from the second trial, TRIUMPH-1-OA, were scheduled for presentation during a separate poster session that same day.

A Potential Latest Treatment for Millions With Knee Osteoarthritis.

Painful knee osteoarthritis affects approximately 5% of Americans (15 million people). Available treatments range from physical therapy and medications applied to the skin to oral anti-inflammatory drugs such as ibuprofen and Voltaren. Other options include opioids and corticosteroid injections, although the relief provided by steroid injections generally lasts only a short time.

Weight loss is another established way to ease symptoms. Previous studies have shown that losing 5% to 10% of body weight through changes in diet and exercise can improve knee osteoarthritis pain. However, Schnitzer explained that losing more than 10% through these approaches alone is often challenging. For people already struggling with painful knees, exercising enough to achieve substantial weight loss can be especially difficult.

In a recent development, retatrutide could offer another approach. Developed by Eli Lilly, the experimental medication is administered as a once-weekly injection and works differently from existing GLP-1 medications such as semaglutide and tirzepatide.

Recent findings suggest that while those drugs act on one or two hormone receptors and typically produce weight reductions of 10% to 20%, retatrutide activates receptors associated with three different naturally occurring hormones. In the clinical trials, participants lost approximately 20% to 25% of their body weight, depending on the dose. Eli Lilly scientists also contributed to the research as study co-authors.

In a recent development, "Participants had remarkable responses," Schnitzer mentioned. "Many of the people in this study lost considerable amounts of weight, with a few losing up to a hundred pounds or more.".

Why Diet and Exercise Still Matter.

Despite the encouraging findings, Schnitzer emphasized that lifestyle changes should remain the starting point for people who are overweight and have painful knee osteoarthritis.

Improving eating habits, increasing physical activity, and making other sustainable lifestyle adjustments can help reduce symptoms without the expense of newer weight-loss medications. These strategies also avoid side effects associated with GLP-1 drugs, including gastrointestinal problems and muscle loss.

Maintaining muscle strength is particularly important for people with knee osteoarthritis because the muscles surrounding the joint help support and stabilize it. Losing too much muscle could therefore create additional challenges for patients who already have difficulty moving comfortably.

In a recent development, for individuals who cannot achieve sufficient weight loss through lifestyle changes and continue to experience significant knee pain, Schnitzer believes retatrutide could become a valuable option if it receives approval from the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.

Could the Drug Also Slow Knee Arthritis Progression?

Although the trials demonstrated substantial improvements in weight and pain, several vital questions remain unanswered.

One of the biggest is whether retatrutide does more than relieve symptoms. Researchers still do not know if the drug can slow the underlying progression of knee osteoarthritis enough to reduce the likelihood that patients will eventually need knee replacement surgery. People who already required a knee replacement were excluded from the trials.

"That would be the goal here to say you can reduce people's pain, and you can stop the progression of their osteoarthritis," Schnitzer mentioned.

Recent findings suggest that another unanswered question is whether retatrutide might benefit people with painful knee osteoarthritis who are not overweight. Because the trials did not include these patients, further studies will be needed to determine whether they could experience similar improvements.

Researchers are also interested in understanding how much of the pain relief comes directly from weight loss and how much might be related to the drug's effects on inflammation.

"These drugs are believed to have significant anti-inflammatory activity, but the mechanism is not entirely known," Schnitzer remarked. "Whether cutting down inflammation in the joint is also vital in addition to reducing load needs more research, so this is still a first step, in my view. I've been working in the OA field for a long time, and I think this opens up opportunities to do a lot more studies to understand the condition better.".

How Researchers Measured Knee Pain Relief.

To evaluate changes in symptoms, the research teams used the Western Ontario and McMaster Universities Arthritis Index (WOMAC) Pain index, a standardized tool for assessing osteoarthritis pain.

During study visits, participants rated their pain on a scale from 0 to 10. They also used a mobile app to record their pain levels each day, allowing researchers to track how symptoms changed throughout treatment.

The study is titled, "Retatrutide Once Weekly in Adults with Knee Osteoarthritis Pain and Obesity.".

💡 Key Takeaways

  • In a recent development, the Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995.
  • Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

A co-living community in West Oakland, CA, has hit the market for the first time.

In a recent development, the Union is a three-house, 14-bedroom compound and is listed at $2,999,995. That’s the asking price for all three homes. If purchased separately by friends, multigenerational families, or any other buyers who want to live side by side, the starting price is $899,000 for the smallest of the three homes, which has five bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Each home is separately deeded as a condo within the greater compound.

This lot has been zoned RM-3, or Mixed Housing Type Residential–3, which allows for multiple single-family homes on a single lot. This setup is permissible due to changes in California law allowing for higher-density housing in residential areas.

This project started in 2019 when a startup called Open Door bought the 7,535-square-foot empty lot and tasked Matt Baran of Baran Studio Architecture with creating a co-living space.

They asked: “What if we design something that can be beautiful design and work with the new state laws that allow for increased density in neighborhoods and works well for community living?” notes listing agent Max Nelson, who specializes in co-living sales through the platform Live Near Friends.

The end result was a rent-by-the-room community where residents enjoyed shared amenities, including a backyard fire pit, co-working space, and rooftop deck with views of downtown Oakland.

The design process balanced group-friendly amenities with the look and feel of the neighborhood, which is filled with mostly Victorian homes.

Nelson says that the architects asked, “How do we create a modern house without making it look like it doesn't fit?”.

The design included bay windows that jut from the homes, mirroring the style of a classic Victorian. Having three separate homes rather than one huge building also matched the aesthetic of the area, as did the incorporation of tall, narrow windows.

Much of the rest of the design leans more modern, especially the efficient energy systems. The homes rely on shared solar panels, greatly reducing energy bills. Everything is electric—there is no reliance on gas. Each room has its own fan coils to create customized comfort.

“It’s a super efficient, well-done system,” says Nelson.

Because The Union was designed for co-living, some of the best features are the shared spaces and the flow among the three homes.

It has been revealed that the property fronting the street, 1514, has the smaller price tag at $899,000 and offers 1,919 square feet of living space, including five bedrooms and four bathrooms. A skybridge connects it with the back two condos, positioned side by side like a duplex and sharing a common wall.

Sources indicate that the larger of the back condos, 1510, is listed at $1,049,500 and sits slightly larger at 2,033 square feet, again with five bedrooms and four bathrooms. Connected is 1512, also offered at $1,049,500 with 2,015 square feet, including four bedrooms and four bathrooms.

Above these two condos is the roof area, which houses the solar panels as well as the communal deck with AstroTurf and several seating areas.

It all adds up to a highly functional, thoughtfully designed compound that meets the needs of communal living. It offers both shared spaces as well as smaller decks, outdoor seating nooks, and private spaces for solo or one-on-one time with another—because shared living works best when people have the freedom to come together or enjoy time apart.

5 Exciting Ways to Invest in Real Estate

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Sources indicate that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth.
  • Industry observers note that in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it.
  • Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Sources indicate that when it comes to exploring enticing investment opportunities, real estate often stands out as an excellent solution for making and growing wealth. No matter how the world around us changes, there will always be a demand for property in attractive areas. This has led countless people to diversify their portfolios over the years, buying rental properties, second homes, and even office spaces.

Industry observers note that in recent years, as the world has continued to evolve, the marketplace for real estate investors has evolved with it. Today, people no longer need to buy and flip entire properties to make money. There are numerous tips for getting started and ways you can start your journey into the property world, and some options are actually simpler and more affordable than you might expect. Here are some of the best, most interesting ways to invest in real estate, if you want to avoid the traditional buy and flip strategy.

Not all real estate investments have to include purchasing actual bricks and mortar in the physical world. The digital landscape has evolved drastically in recent years, introducing newly introduced opportunities for innovative entrepreneurs to make money buying virtual assets. As the concept of the metaverse continues to gain traction, digital real estate is growing increasingly attractive.

Sources indicate that with digital real estate, companies purchase a section of the blockchain in a metaverse landscape, where they can build online experiences, or simply store other assets. In 2021, sales on four of the biggest metaverse platforms for real estate reached a whopping $501 million. This indicates learning how to invest in digital real estate could be a worthwhile strategy for any consumer. Not only is it potentially profitable, but the digital real estate also requires less work to manage and maintain than a physical house or property.

Even if you’re not familiar with this form of property-based investing, you probably know the term crowdfunding. Made popular by sites like GoFundMe and Kickstarter, the crowdfunding strategy involves individuals pooling their resources together to fund a product or business. In the real estate world, investors can work together to purchase a property, such as a corporate space, warehouse, or block of flats, reducing the initial cost of a purchase.

The approach allows investors to participate in products that would have been impossible to access in the past because of high capital requirements. Individuals can use this strategy to diversify their portfolios with a variety of different locations and property types. Plus, you’ll earn a passive income through rental profits, and property appreciation.

Another real estate investment strategy gaining increasing attention in recent years is REITs. These are basically investment vehicles responsible for owning and operating income-generating assets, such as rental properties and office blocks. They’re traded on traditional stock exchanges and provide individuals with an opportunity to invest in the market, without directly owning a property or having to manage the investment themselves.

Industry observers note that REITs can come with several attractive features, including regular distributions of dividends, and the ability to explore a range of different sectors. You can even use this strategy to spread your portfolio across industrial, residential, and commercial properties. They’re also a highly liquid investment option, making them appealing to beginners.

Finally, one interesting way to invest in real estate, without buying a physical property outright, is to spend some of your money on shares in PropTech startups. PropTech, or Property Technology startups, are companies focused on developing tools and real estate designed to transform the property landscape. They develop things like property management solutions, smart home technology, and virtual reality applications for tours.

According to recent reports, if you already have experience in the world of stocks and shares, investing in a PropTech company could be an excellent way to utilize your existing knowledge and diversify your portfolio. It’s also a chance to get your foot in the door with a company that’s actively disrupting the real estate space, and the market as we know it.

Industry observers note that investing in property has become a much more diverse and versatile opportunity for individuals in recent years. No matter how much money you can afford to spend, or where your expertise lies, you can find plenty of ways to expand your portfolio with disruptive real-estate investment strategies.
